articles.title: Inside Trump’s deal to give American taxpayer's a massive stake in new $6.6B submarine deal
articles.summary: President Donald Trump announced a 40% taxpayer stake in Anduril's Arsenal-2 shipyard subsidiary, adding government ownership to the $6.6 billion deal.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — New details of President Donald Trump's multibillion-dollar deal with a defense tech giant reveal that the U.S. government will own 40% of the firm holding its new submarine shipyard without controlling it. But first, Anduril must prove it can build Navy-certified components before competing for future production work, a U.S. official told Fox News Digital. The government will use authorities under the Defense Production Act and the Pentagon's Industrial Base Fund to acquire its stake in a newly formed company holding the Arsenal-2 shipyard in Baltimore, Maryland. The official described it as a "minority, non-control" investment designed to secure "tangible ownership and long-term value for American taxpayers." Fox News Digital has asked the Department of War for the dollar value of the investment. The Navy's up-to-$2.9 billion agreement is not a guarantee of future submarine production work for Anduril. The money will flow through General Dynamics Electric Boat, the Navy's lead Virginia-class submarine builder, and calls for Anduril to fabricate and qualify four test components. Anduril is separately committing $3.7 billion of its own capital to the project. Anduril is not guaranteed future production work. Instead, Electric Boat will set the specifications and oversee testing, qualification and Navy certification. If Anduril meets those milestones, it will have "the opportunity, but not the entitlement, to compete for future production work," the official said. "The ultimate proof of our commitment to ensuring the shipyard's enduring success: American taxpayers will receive a 40 percent stake in the new shipyard," Trump said Tuesday at Sparrows Point shipyard. "We get 40 percent." STARTUPS BRING INNOVATION TO DEFENSE INDUSTRIAL BASE The size of the stake stands out even as the Trump administration has increasingly taken direct government interests in companies and projects it considers critical to national security. The administration has struck equity arrangements involving chipmaker Intel, rare earths producer MP Materials and other strategic industries. The arrangement is part of a broader $6.6 billion effort to expand production of Virginia-class attack submarines as the U.S. struggles to keep pace with China's vast shipbuilding capacities and the Navy falls behind on its production goal. Anduril is committing $3.7 billion of its own capital to build the facility and manufacturing capacity, while the Navy could spend up to $2.9 billion purchasing what it produces. The project is aimed at closing a persistent U.S. submarine production shortfall as China rapidly expands its naval and shipbuilding capacity. American shipyards are delivering roughly 1.3 Virginia-class attack submarines a year, short of the Navy's goal of two, which it does not expect to reach until around 2032. Once fully operational, Arsenal-2 is expected to add about 9 million labor hours annually to the submarine industrial base, increasing Virginia-class production capacity by roughly 15%, an administration official told reporters on a call before Trump’s remarks. LARGEST-EVER US STEEL PLANT IS COMING TO A KEY RED STATE AS TRUMP UNVEILS $15B INVESTMENT An industry official on the call emphasized that Anduril would finance the new production capacity itself while the government paid for the resulting output. "I wouldn't say that the government's paying us back. We feel the government [is] buying the results of what we're able to produce," the industry official said. The 40% government stake was not disclosed on the call, which included questions from reporters about how the project would be financed. The submarine crunch is part of a broader shipbuilding gap with China, whose vast commercial maritime industry also supports its rapidly expanding navy. China now accounts for more than half of global commercial shipbuilding output, while the U.S. accounts for only a fraction of 1%, giving Beijing an enormous industrial base that can also support military ship construction. Anduril plans to begin with critical components including torpedo tubes, which a senior administration official described as a current "gating component" slowing Virginia-class production. The company eventually plans to manufacture larger modules and sections of submarines at Arsenal-2. articles.title: Site oferece criptomoeda a quem divulgar conteúdo pró-Flávio Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Especialistas apontam indícios de irregularidades na iniciativa Brasil 22 Token, divulgada em um perfil de crianças de Uganda com 12,9 milhões de seguidores no Instagram.
articles.summary: Especialistas apontam indícios de irregularidades na iniciativa Brasil 22 Token, divulgada em um perfil de crianças de Uganda com 12,9 milhões de seguidores no Instagram.
articles.body:
Site do Brasil 22, de criptomoedas, apresenta suas duas principais frentes de atuação: o apoio à conclusão da Casa das HypersKids, em Kampala, e o posicionamento do movimento em favor do voto em Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) — Foto: Reprodução

Um site que vende criptomoedas está oferecendo tokens (ativos digitais que podem ser transferidos e trocados por dinheiro) a quem participar de uma campanha que promete ajudar crianças de Uganda e divulgar nas redes sociais uma "comunidade" que defende abertamente o voto em Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que disputará o 2º turno da eleição presidencial com Lula (PT) em 25 de outubro.

A iniciativa "Brasil 22 Token (B22)" foi lançada na terça-feira (6), segundo reportagem publicada nesta quinta (8) pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo, e é promovida no Instagram pelo perfil @hyperskidsafrica, de crianças ugandenses, que tem 12,9 milhões de seguidores e aparece no site de criptomoedas como "parceira oficial".

Um post no Instagram que mostra crianças dançando com a camiseta da campanha incentiva a compra da criptomoeda $B22 e cita o próprio Flávio Bolsonaro, o deputado federal Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG) e Pablo Marçal (PRTB), que tentou concorrer a presidente, mas foi barrado pela Justiça e hoje apoia Flávio.

"Recebemos 120 milhões de tokens $B22 por meio desta parceria! Um movimento que apoia a HypersKids e acredita em um Brasil melhor. Apoiamos a visão de @nikolasferreiradm, @flaviobolsonaro e @pablomarcal1. Junte-se a nós: compre $B22, compartilhe nas suas redes sociais e acesse o site para saber como ganhar tokens inspirando outras pessoas a votar 22!", diz o post no Instagram das crianças.

O site da campanha Brasil 22 diz que se trata de "um movimento que une apoio ao voto 22 e a proposta de ajudar as HypersKids a concluir sua casa em Kampala".

A lei eleitoral veda oferecer vantagem econômica a quem divulga propaganda eleitoral na internet e proíbe empresas de doar recursos para campanhas eleitorais e candidatos, inclusive com criptomoedas . Três especialistas ouvidos pelo g1 apontam indícios de violação da lei na campanha Brasil 22 Token divulgada no perfil das crianças de Uganda.

Um texto publicado no site Brasil 22 diz que o "apoio ao voto 22 é uma posição do próprio Brasil 22 Token" e que não há vínculo com partidos, políticos, candidaturas ou campanhas eleitorais. Afirma também que não há "garantia de retorno financeiro" e que a distribuição de tokens é "independente de voto, preferência eleitoral ou divulgação de propaganda eleitoral".

O professor de direito eleitoral Fernando Neisser, da Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV), afirma que o fato de o site negar ligação com a campanha não muda o enquadramento da conduta. Na visão dele, "a conduta é absolutamente ilegal, tendo ou não relação direta com a campanha".

Ele explica que o caso viola, ao mesmo tempo, três regras. Duas delas decorrem da proibição de que empresas façam campanha ou doem a candidatos, em vigor desde 2015, quando o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) vetou o financiamento empresarial . A terceira trata da premiação por divulgação, que o professor diz ter ficado mais explícita na regulamentação da Justiça Eleitoral depois do caso do ex-candidato Pablo Marçal nas eleições municipais de 2024.

"Viola, a um só tempo, três regras. Trata-se de página de pessoa jurídica fazendo campanha para candidato, constitui com isso doação estimável em dinheiro de PJ [pessoa jurídica] para candidato, e promove campanha envolvendo monetização e premiação, o que já era proibido, mas agora ainda mais claramente na resolução depois do caso Marçal", diz o professor da FGV.

Marçal foi condenado pela Justiça Eleitoral e ficou inelegível após promover campeonatos em que seguidores que distribuíam mais "cortes" para promover sua candidatura a prefeito de São Paulo em 2024 concorriam a prêmios em dinheiro.

No caso da campanha para promover o B22, o regulamento diz que, para se inscrever até 26 de outubro, às 23h59, o participante precisa manter ao menos 10 mil B22 em carteira digital e fazer uma publicação no X, no Instagram ou no TikTok mostrando que faz parte da "comunidade B22". A postagem precisa continuar no ar até a distribuição dos tokens, que ocorre em até sete dias após a aprovação.

O regulamento não exige que o post peça voto explicitamente em Flávio Bolsonaro. O site, porém, afirma defender o voto 22 como posição do movimento.

Para o advogado Matheus Puppe, mestre e doutorando em Direito Digital pela Universidade de Frankfurt e consultor da Comissão Especial de Direito Digital da Câmara dos Deputados, o fato de a recompensa ser paga em criptoativos não cria exceção à regra eleitoral.

Para ele, o ponto central é saber se o participante recebe o ativo porque publicou ou compartilhou propaganda eleitoral, e é isso que a Justiça Eleitoral deveria examinar, e não os avisos do site.

"Se essa relação existir, expressões como 'comunidade', 'meme', 'causa social' ou 'projeto independente' não neutralizam a irregularidade. A Justiça Eleitoral deve examinar o funcionamento real da operação, e não apenas o aviso colocado no rodapé do site", diz Puppe.

O presidente da OAB de Rondônia, Márcio Nogueira, também especialista em direito eleitoral e digital, faz a mesma ressalva: a ilegalidade depende de ficar provado que os tokens estão condicionados à divulgação de conteúdo favorável a um candidato. Para ele, se isso ocorrer, a Justiça Eleitoral tem fundamento para agir.

"A legislação eleitoral proíbe a oferta de vantagens econômicas a usuários para estimular a publicação de propaganda político-eleitoral na internet", diz Nogueira.

Segundo ele, quem organiza e financia a iniciativa pode ser investigado e sofrer sanções eleitorais, como multa e ordem para retirar a propaganda irregular. O mesmo vale para a responsabilidade do candidato, que a lei condiciona à prova. A Lei das Eleições exige que a representação contra o beneficiário demonstre autoria ou prévio conhecimento da propaganda irregular, e Nogueira afirma que o simples benefício eleitoral não basta. Puppe converge com essa visão:

"Para multar o candidato beneficiado por essa modalidade de propaganda, é necessário comprovar seu prévio conhecimento. A mera existência de uma iniciativa que o favoreça não permite presumir que ele a organizou ou autorizou."

O que a lei permite, na avaliação dos especialistas, é o apoio espontâneo e gratuito de eleitores a candidatos nas próprias redes, e a doação de pessoas físicas dentro dos limites legais, pela conta oficial da campanha. Fora disso, para Puppe, o risco é transformar mobilização em mercado.

"O risco é criar um mercado de engajamento eleitoral em que a remuneração aparece disfarçada de mobilização espontânea", diz Puppe.

A conta de Flávio Bolsonaro aparece entre as que seguem o @hyperskidsafrica. Seguir um perfil, por si só, não comprova ligação com a campanha nem conhecimento prévio do conteúdo. A campanha foi procurada pelo g1 , mas não respondeu até a publicação da reportagem. O Brasil22 e hyperskidsafrica também foram procurados. O espaço segue aberto para manifestações.

articles.title: Bahia elegeu 58 pretos e pardos; Santa Catarina não elegeu nenhum | G1
articles.standfirst: Dados do TSE mostram que pretos ou pardos foram 49,9% dos candidatos nas eleições de 2026. Entre os eleitos, a proporção é de 29,9%.
articles.summary: Dados do TSE mostram que pretos e pardos foram 49,9% dos candidatos nas eleições de 2026. Entre os eleitos, a proporção é de 29,9%.
articles.body:
Dos 1.774 candidatos eleitos neste 1º turno de eleições, 531 são pretos ou pardos. A proporção, segundo dados do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), é de 29,9% em relação ao total.

🔎 Nas eleições de 2026, foram registradas 10.224 candidaturas de pessoas pretas ou pardas (49,9%), ante 9.974 de pessoas brancas (48,7%), em um total de 20.496 registros. Os cargos em disputa e considerados neste levantamento são de presidente, governador, senador, deputado federal e deputado estadual ou distrital.

O estado que mais elegeu candidatos pretos ou pardos, em números absolutos, foi a Bahia , com 58 candidatos; seguida por Minas Gerais, com 38 candidatos; e pelo Rio de Janeiro , com 34. Respectivamente, os estados representam o 4º, 2º e 3º maiores colégios eleitorais do Brasil.

Entre os que menos elegeram, também em números absolutos, está Santa Catarina , que não elegeu nenhum candidato preto ou pardo; seguido por Alagoas , que elegeu cinco candidatos; e o Paraná , com seis.

As candidaturas pretas e pardas eleitas no país conquistaram cargos de governador (5 eleitos), vice-governador (4), senador (15), deputado federal (117), deputado distrital (9), deputado estadual (213) e suplente (39).

Levantamento do g1 mostra, em números absolutos, os candidatos pretos e pardos eleitos nos diferentes estados do Brasil — Foto: g1

No recorte de gênero, 407 homens pretos ou pardos foram eleitos. As mulheres somam 124. Proporcionalmente, representam 28,9% e 33,6% do total de homens e mulheres eleitos, respectivamente.

O partido que mais elegeu candidatos pretos ou pardos foi o PT, com 83 candidaturas. Em seguida aparecem o PL, com 73, e o União Brasil, com 54.

DC, Democrata, Missão, Mobiliza e Rede não elegeram nenhum. Todos os partidos tinham candidatos pretos ou pardos disputando a eleição. Cidadania e Solidariedade elegeram um candidato preto ou pardo cada.

Candidatos pretos e pardos eleitos por partido no Brasil — Foto: g1

Proporção de pretos e pardos entre eleitos

No Amazonas, dos 38 eleitos, 24 são pretos ou pardos (63,2%). No Tocantins, o grupo conquistou 22 vagas, no total de 38 eleitos (57,9%). No Amapá, pretos e pardos representam 55% dos eleitos (22 de 40).

Na outra ponta, estão os três estados da Região Sul: Santa Catarina, que não elegeu nenhum candidato preto ou pardo de 64 eleitos; Paraná, que tem 6 ante 92 eleitos (6,5%); e o Rio Grande do Sul, com 7 ante 94 eleitos (7,4%).

Cor ou raça dos eleitos proporcionamente nos estados — Foto: g1

De acordo com dados do Censo 2022 do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística ( IBGE ), pretos e pardos são 55,1% da população. Esse percentual é maior do que o de pessoas com essas características eleitas, de 29,9%.

articles.title: Quantos votos teve Lula no primeiro turno? | G1
articles.standfirst: Nestas eleições de 2026, Flávio teve 56,1 milhões de votos (47,03%), e Lula, 53,8 milhões (45,16%).
articles.summary: Nestas eleições de 2026, Flávio teve 56,1 milhões de votos (47,03%), e Lula, 53,8 milhões (45,16%).
articles.body:
Presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) em pronunciamento após o 1º turno das eleições — Foto: Foto: Ricardo Stuckert

Lula (PT) recebeu 53.879.538 votos, correspondendo a 45,16% dos votos válidos no primeiro turno das Eleições 2026.

Já Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) terminou o primeiro turno na liderança, com 56.104.268 votos, 47,03% dos válidos.

A diferença entre os dois foi de 2.227.651 votos. Em 2022, a situação era inversa. Lula havia terminado o primeiro turno à frente, com 57.259.504 votos (48,43%), contra 51.072.345 (43,20%) de Jair Bolsonaro . Uma vantagem de 6.187.159 votos do petista.

Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro disputam o segundo turno no dia 25 de setembro . Apenas cinco estados e o Distrito Federal terão disputa de governador em 2º turno.

Flávio Bolsonaro foi o candidato mais votado em 14 estados e no Distrito Federal, enquanto Lula ficou na frente em 12 estados. Em comparação com a disputa entre Lula e Jair Bolsonaro em 2022, dois estados mudaram de lado. Minas Gerais e Tocantins, que haviam dado maioria a Lula quatro anos antes, passaram para Flávio.

Comparativo de votações no 1º turno nos estados - 2022 e 2026 — Foto: Arte g1

A mudança mais relevante em números absolutos aconteceu em Minas Gerais. Em 2022, Lula recebeu 5.802.571 votos, contra 5.239.264 de Jair Bolsonaro — uma vantagem petista de 563.307 votos.

Em 2026, Lula caiu para 5.188.936 votos (43,33%) em Minas, enquanto Flávio chegou a 5.777.548 (48,24%). A vantagem passou a ser de 588.612 votos para Flávio. Ou seja, Lula perdeu 613.635 votos no estado, enquanto Flávio obteve 538.284 a mais que o pai.

Em Tocantins, a mudança foi menor em números absolutos, mas também suficiente para inverter o resultado. Lula passou de 434.303 votos em 2022 para 404.009 em 2026, enquanto o candidato bolsonarista passou de 379.194 votos com Jair para 469.321 com Flávio. Assim, uma vantagem de 55.109 votos para Lula em 2022 virou uma diferença de 65.312 para Flávio em 2026.

articles.title: STF considera válida lei do Paraná que amplia tempo mínimo de estacionamento gratuito para pessoas com deficiência | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministros consideraram que lei estadual que fixa 30 minutos de permanência livre não viola princípios constitucionais e pode ser proposta pelo Legislativo.
articles.summary: Ministros consideraram que lei estadual que fixa 30 minutos de permanência livre não viola princípios constitucionais e pode ser proposta pelo Legislativo.
articles.body:
Vaga para pessoas com deficiência — Foto: Andrzej Rembowski por Pixabay

O Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) decidiu nesta quinta-feira (8), por unanimidade, que é constitucional lei estadual que amplia tempo mínimo de permanência gratuita para pessoas com deficiência em estacionamentos privados.

O relator, ministro Nunes Marques, entendeu que o objetivo imediato da legislação é assegurar condições de acessibilidade e inclusão social às pessoas com deficiência que utilizem veículos para acessar estabelecimentos abertos ao público.

O ministro afirmou que a lei não pretendeu regular o preço dos estacionamentos, ou seja, não regulou a forma de exploração econômica de propriedade privada, o que violaria a competência legislativa privativa da União Federal ( leia mais abaixo) .

Ele foi acompanhado pelos ministros Dias Toffoli, Flávio Dino, André Mendonça, Cristiano Zanin, Alexandre de Moraes, Luiz Fux e o presidente da Corte, Edson Fachin.

Os ministros analisaram uma ação da Associação Brasileira de Shopping Centers (Abrasce).

A organização contestou uma lei do Paraná que fixou período mínimo de gratuidade de 30 minutos –o dobro do período de gratuidade já concedido aos demais veículos – para pessoas com deficiência.

Para a Abrasce, a lei deveria ter sido proposta pela União e não pela assembleia legislativa estadual, porque pretende regular a forma de exploração econômica de propriedade privada, matéria que se enquadra no ramo do Direito Civil.

A associação levantou ainda precedentes para sustentar que o STF já tinha decidido no sentido de que a gratuidade, isenção, limitação de preços e cobrança proporcional ao tempo da utilização de estacionamento envolve matéria de direito civil reservada à União.

A Abrasce argumentou também que a lei violou o direito de propriedade e os princípios constitucionais da livre iniciativa e da livre concorrência.

Lei do Paraná que fixou período mínimo de gratuidade de 30 minutos, ou o dobro do período de gratuidade já concedido aos demais veículos, para pessoas com deficiência — Foto: Pâmela Fernandes/G1

Nunes Marques rebateu o argumento da Abrasce que considerou que o Legislativo do Paraná usurpou a competência da União ao tentar disciplinar a exploração econômica de estacionamentos.

Para o relator, as normas questionadas não tratam do regime jurídico da propriedade, nem estabelecem regras gerais sobre contratos civis.

“Seu objetivo imediato é assegurar condições de acessibilidade e inclusão social às pessoas com deficiência que utilizem veículos automotores para acessar estabelecimentos abertos ao público”, afirmou o relator.

Nunes Marques destacou que o Poder Legislativo paranaense não pretendeu regular o preço dos estacionamentos, mas sim assegurar que o tempo adicional necessário à utilização do estacionamento por pessoas com deficiência não fossem um obstáculo econômico ao uso do serviço em condições iguais às demais pessoas.

O ministro do STF Kassio Nunes Marques — Foto: Rosinei Coutinho/STF

“Convém observar ainda que o direito à acessibilidade não se limita à eliminação de barreiras estritamente físicas ou arquitetônicas. As dificuldades de utilização de instalações e serviços abertos ao público podem apresentar manifestações diversas, conforme a natureza da deficiência e sua interação com o ambiente”.

O ministro Alexandre de Moraes afirmou que é razoável que a pessoa com deficiência tenha mais tempo sem pagar no estacionamento.

“Se ela gasta mais tempo em virtude das suas condições físicas, ela tem que ter um tempo proporcional para isso. É exatamente essa a previsão. Sejamos objetivos e sinceros. Nenhum estacionamento, nenhum shopping, nenhuma loja vai quebrar por causa disso”, afirmou Moraes.

“Eu estou acompanhando integralmente sua excelência, o relator, do ponto de vista material. Entendo que a obrigação criada é adequada, necessária e razoável”, concluiu Fachin.

articles.title: The politics of tariffs after Trump
articles.summary: Trump’s most enduring legacy on trade may be not the tariffs themselves, but the partisan realignment they leave behind.
articles.body:
President Trump appears to have turned Democrats into tariff skeptics. Is this just partisan opposition? Perhaps. But Democrats are not just talking about the costs of his tariffs. They are also challenging the presidential powers used to impose them. That points to a potentially more durable realignment in U.S. trade politics, one that rewriting the statutes could help make stick.

On the campaign trail, Democrats are quick to point out that Trump’s tariffs raise costs and undermine “affordability.” No surprise there. Most Americans agree with this view. A January Council on Foreign Relations-Morning Consult poll found that more than 65 percent of respondents believed tariffs made everyday goods less affordable.

But Democrats increasingly take their critique a step further, looking past the tariffs themselves to Trump’s whack-a-mole strategy for preserving them. After the Supreme Court rejected Trump’s use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose sweeping tariffs, the administration pivoted to other statutes.

But this strategy has also been challenged. In May, the Court of International Trade held that Trump’s 10 percent tariffs exceeded the authority Congress had delegated under Section 122 , rejecting the administration’s effort to equate the U.S. trade deficit with the “large and serious” balance of payments problem envisioned by the statute. That decision has been stayed pending appeal.

Trump’s Section 301 “forced labor” tariffs are also under legal review . The Court of International Trade recently questioned whether the government had established the necessary nexus between the conduct of each targeted country and the statutory basis for imposing tariffs. Without that nexus, Section 301 risks becoming a permanent trade war powers authority rather than the targeted remedy Congress enacted.

These cases test the boundaries of the tariff powers Congress delegated to the executive. Democrats are going a step further, asking whether Congress drew those boundaries too broadly.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, gave the broadest answer in July. His Congressional Trade Powers Reform Act of 2026 would require congressional approval of new presidential tariffs, establish a bipartisan Joint Committee on Tariffs and Trade to review proposed actions, require congressional approval of trade agreements and increase congressional oversight of the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative.

Wyden explicitly described the objective as reversing executive overreach and putting Congress “back in the driver’s seat” on trade. In September, Senate Democrats offered three proposals that push further in that direction.

Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) focused on Canada. Her resolution targets Trump’s use of Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose tariffs on Canadian goods. It argues that the duties increase costs for American consumers and businesses, disrupt integrated North American supply chains and invite Canadian retaliation. It calls on Trump to rescind the tariffs.

Rosen and Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) expand upon this with their BAD DEAL Act . Rather than reversing the Canada tariffs, their bill would repeal Section 338 itself, nullify presidential actions taken under it and refund duties already collected.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) went further still. His End Trump’s Tariff Tax Act would terminate the administration’s Section 301 forced labor tariffs, repeal Sections 122 and 338 and automatically refund duties with interest.

For now, these proposals are political markers. But political markers have a way of becoming policy agendas. And this agenda poses different questions for the two parties.

For Republicans, how much of Trump’s tariff regime are they willing to defend? They’ve been falling back on the argument that tariffs provide negotiating leverage and protect domestic industries. But as courts narrow executive authorities, the middle ground shrinks. Republicans may have to choose between rewriting the statutes to preserve presidential discretion or accepting a larger congressional role.

There are signs of unease among congressional Republicans, some of whom have opposed some Trump tariffs or called for more congressional oversight . After Trump exits the political stage, Phil Gramm and Donald Boudreaux argue Republicans may even revert to their traditional preference for lower tariffs and open markets.

Democrats face the same question. If their principal objection to Trump’s tariffs concerns presidential discretion, clawing back congressional authority may be enough. Tariffs would remain instruments of economic policy, but Congress would exercise much greater control over their use. Court rulings will make that choice harder to avoid.

But if their critique is that tariffs raise prices, increase input costs and disrupt supply chains, the challenge after Trump will be to determine when tariffs remain useful and how to deploy them without reproducing the economic costs Democrats are warning about today.

Trump has scrambled the politics of U.S. trade policy. The question is whether the parties scramble back once Trump leaves office. If they don’t, Trump’s most enduring legacy on trade may be not the tariffs themselves, but the partisan realignment they leave behind.

Marc L. Busch is the Karl F. Landegger Professor of International Business Diplomacy at the Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University.

articles.title: 30 percent of Trump voters enthusiastic about casting ballots: Survey
articles.summary: Fewer voters who backed President Trump in 2024 than those who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris say they are “very enthusiastic” to cast ballots in November, according to new polling. The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey, released Thursday, found 30 percent of Trump voters said they are “very enthusiastic” to vote in the midterms, while…
articles.body:
Fewer voters who backed President Trump in 2024 than those who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris say they are “very enthusiastic” to cast ballots in November, according to new polling.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey , released Thursday, found 30 percent of Trump voters said they are “very enthusiastic” to vote in the midterms, while 21 percent shared a moderate rate of excitement. Just less than 10 percent were lukewarm about voting, and 10 percent said they are “very” unenthusiastic. Another 30 percent said they are neither enthusiastic nor unenthusiastic or skipped the question.

By comparison, 48 percent of Harris voters said they are “very enthusiastic” to vote in November, followed by 18 percent who were just enthusiastic. Fewer Harris voters were unenthusiastic to vote, with 7 percent lukewarm and 6 percent “very” unenthusiastic. About 20 percent said they are neither or did not answer.

These results came days after the pollsters found Trump’s approval rating remained steady at 32 percent since its September poll, with 65 percent saying they do not approve of his handling of the presidency.

Gains that Trump made with support from Hispanic voters in states like Texas in 2024 have also been on the decline, with 24 percent of respondents previously telling the polling firm they approve of Trump’s job performance. GOP candidates fare slightly better, with 26 percent of Hispanic voters saying they back Republican candidates seeking wins in November.

The drop-off in the president’s support has cast a dark shadow over Republican prospects going into the midterms as Trump continues to urge voters to pretend he is “ on the ballot ” in the election.

He has also tried to downplay concerns over rising gas prices over the course of the Iran war as it stretches into its eighth month. He has said the high cost of gas is a “ very inexpensive price to pay ” to prevent the regime from developing and obtaining a nuclear weapon.

The president similarly said so at a Nebraska rally on Monday when he said the Iranian regime could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego, enraging California Democrats who called on him to apologize. California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said the remark rises to the level of invoking the 25th Amendment . Trump doubled down on the comments on Wednesday evening.

The possibility that the Iran war could cost Trump and Republicans one or both chambers of Congress is one the president has raised on the campaign trail. Earlier this month, he told reporters that the conflict “should help” his party’s chances.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey was conducted Sept. 30 through Oct. 5 and included 2,848 respondents with a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

articles.title: GOP accuses Walz allies of burying $52M Medicaid fraud report before election
articles.summary: Minnesota Republicans accuse Democrats of blocking the full Optum Medicaid fraud report, but DFL lawmakers say DHS has failed to provide it.
articles.body: Minnesota Republicans are accusing Democrats of keeping lawmakers in the dark for months about a state-commissioned Medicaid assessment that flagged more than $52 million in improper payments, arguing the delay denied them a chance to act on the report’s specific findings during the legislative session before the election. "Fraud here has exploded under the Walz administration," Minnesota Republican Speaker of the House Lisa Demuth told Fox News Digital. "Governor Walz has held no one in his entire administration accountable for the level of fraud. It definitely brings into question what is in that report and why are they hiding it?" The Walz administration hired Optum to conduct a third-party review of Minnesota’s Medicaid program, scrutinizing 14 high-risk services. The report identified more than $52 million in improper payments but cautioned that improper payments do not necessarily constitute "fraud, waste or abuse." The Department of Human Services released a heavily redacted version to the public in February, prompting calls from Republican lawmakers to make the full version available so they could address the risks raised during the legislative session. "Our election here in Minnesota is 29 days away. We’re just four weeks out, and you really have to wonder why they are refusing to do this," Demuth, who is the GOP gubernatorial candidate, told Fox News Digital. WALZ ADMINISTRATION IGNORED FRAUD WARNINGS AS BILLIONS VANISHED, HOUSE OVERSIGHT REPORT ALLEGES Minnesota currently has a divided state legislature, with the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL) holding a slim 34-33 majority in the Senate and a rare 67-67 partisan tie in the House. Democratic Gov. Tim Walz announced the audit in October 2025, months before allegations of widespread fraud involving members of Minnesota’s Somali diaspora drew national attention. Mounting scrutiny of the Walz administration’s handling of alleged fraud in Minnesota’s social services programs contributed to growing political pressure before Walz ended his re-election campaign in January. WALZ'S 'EXIT INTERVIEW' REFLECTING ON HIS TENURE SPARKS LAWMAKER DEBATE ABOUT HIS LEGACY: 'NEVER SERIOUS' Republican state Sen. Jordan Rasmusson is also accusing the Walz administration and his Democratic counterparts of seeking to "minimize" the fraud issue in the state. "I think it’s really hard for Democrats, elected Democrats in Minnesota, to admit that we have a fraud problem of this scale, and to take accountability for those failings," Rasmusson told Fox News Digital. The Department of Human Services said the report was heavily redacted to protect Optum’s trade secrets and prevent the release of sensitive security information that could provide criminals a "roadmap" for committing fraud. Rasmusson introduced an amendment in April to make the full Optum report public, but it failed along party lines. A version of Rasmusson's provision was later passed in May as part of a broader budget package. MINNESOTA'S ANTI-ICE AID FUND BECOMES LATEST CASUALTY OF STATE'S EMBARRASSING FRAUD PROBLEM Under the law, DHS must provide the initial Optum reports to members of a legislative committee with "jurisdiction over human services policy and finance" following a joint request from the committee’s chair and ranking minority member. Lawmakers may review the report but cannot publicly release protected nonpublic information it contains. Rasmusson said he issued a request for the full report in June. State Rep. Mohamud Noor, DFL co-chair of the Human Services Finance and Policy Committee, and former GOP House co-Chair Joe Schomacker requested the report in May. The report did not become available to a select group of lawmakers until last week. "I'm grateful that it's out, but it's very disappointing we couldn’t have returned to St. Paul to address it," Republican state Rep. Dawn Gillman told Fox News Digital, noting that lawmakers will have to wait until January to address the report. "The broader takeaway is that the Walz administration could have given us more access to those months ago," Rasmusson told Fox News Digital. "Legislative Democrats could have joined Republicans and got access to this information months ago during session." However, state Sen. John Hoffman, who now has access to the report, pushed back on the notion that lawmakers needed full access to enact meaningful changes. "This is a report about vulnerabilities in public programs," Hoffman said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Why would we release that to the public before we fixed them? We wouldn’t publish a report about which banks don’t lock their doors, either." EXPLOSIVE SLEEPER ISSUE COULD FUEL MIDTERM SHAKEUPS, TOP REPUBLICAN PREDICTS: ‘YOU’RE GONNA SEE SURPRISES’ "The rest of us got to work passing legislation to ensure high-quality services, continuity of care for people in need and safeguards to protect against fraud," Hoffman continued. "Having reviewed the report, I can tell you it is already outdated, and the gaps and weaknesses it raises have already been addressed by laws we passed this year." But Rasmusson, who also has the report, disagreed with Hoffman. "After reviewing the unredacted Optum report, my main takeaway is that it underscores the systemic failures of the Walz administration and Minnesota Democrats to protect Minnesota from fraud," Rasmusson told Fox News Digital. "Whether it is issues with determining the eligibility of program recipients, determining whether providers are actually providing real services or not, or even some of the basic analytics that would catch fraud, Minnesota is very far behind where it should be in program integrity initiatives," Rasmusson continued. Fox News Digital reached out to DHS, which confirmed that select lawmakers now had the report. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "We appreciate legislators' interest in receiving a copy of the unredacted initial Optum report from February 2026," Minnesota Department of Human Services Temporary Commissioner John Connolly said in a statement. "In alignment with the law passed by the Legislature last session, the Minnesota Department of Human Services released the Optum reports last week." articles.title: Bipartisan Senate duo proposes filibuster rules reform to fix gridlock
articles.summary: Sens. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) have teamed up in calling for several major reforms to the Senate rules that they say are needed to restore bipartisanship and bring the slow-moving institution into the modern age. “Both our parties have been hamstrung by the Senate’s tangled rules,” they wrote in a joint op-ed…
articles.body:
Sens. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) have teamed up in calling for several major reforms to the Senate rules that they say are needed to restore bipartisanship and bring the slow-moving institution into the modern age.

“Both our parties have been hamstrung by the Senate’s tangled rules,” they wrote in a joint op-ed for The Washington Post. “The world isn’t waiting for the Senate. Technology and the global economy are changing faster than ever before. The Senate needs to be able to keep up to legislate effectively.”

The senators argue that colleagues are abusing the rules by dragging out floor consideration of even routine or robustly bipartisan bills for days to gain leverage for their own pet issues.

They say some of the worst abuse has come in the form of frivolous filibusters that require 60 votes and days to set aside.

“Cloture was created in 1917 as a tool for the Senate to end filibusters and start voting. But the 60-vote threshold generally required for a cloture motion to pass is now deliberately abused to slow down the legislative process and delay voting on big issues,” Daines and Merkley wrote.

Daines and Merkley are proposing eliminating cloture votes — which need the support of 60 senators to pass — on what they’re calling “routine business” such as nominations, amendments and motions to proceed to business on the floor.

They want to get rid of the “intervening day” — the full calendar day that is required to pass between when a cloture motion is first filed and when the Senate votes on it.

They want to shrink the “post-cloture” time that is now required under the rules to elapse on major business after the Senate has invoked cloture to end debate and before a final vote is held. Senators now must wait up to 30 hours on major items before proceeding to a final vote.

The senators also proposed a fast-track process for considering bills on the Senate floor that pass out of committee with strong bipartisan support, noting that more than 650 bipartisan bills have passed out of committee but haven’t received any floor time because of time and procedural constraints. Under this new expedited process, if a bill passes out of committee with the support of a majority of Republican and Democratic senators, it would be eligible for passage on the Senate floor with a simple majority after six hours of debate.

Doing so would require the bill’s supporters to gather the signatures of 16 senators, including at least one from each party, on a petition.

Daines and Merkley say there should also be a two-day fast track for bipartisan spending bills.

Appropriations bills on an expedited path would need to be accompanied by a list of 20 relevant amendments, 10 amendments from each side of the aisle, and each amendment would be subject to only five minutes of debate.

They argued that the Senate has already “recognized the need for fast-track procedures” by using expedited floor procedures several times this Congress to repeal executive branch-imposed rules under the Congressional Review Act and to pass major legislation through the budget reconciliation process.

“For too long, the Senate has been stuck in the muck. Our bipartisan plan will get it moving by letting senators debate, negotiate and legislate again so we can deliver for the American people,” they wrote.

articles.title: A rare healthcare issue both parties agree on: A solution to Alzheimer’s that can’t wait
articles.summary: Bipartisan legislators introduced the ASAP Act to authorize Medicare coverage for FDA-approved blood-based biomarker tests aimed at the early detection of Alzheimer’s and other dementias.
articles.body:
As members of Congress on opposite sides of the aisle, we don’t see eye-to-eye on everything. But Alzheimer’s disease doesn’t care about politics. It affects families in every state, congressional district and neighborhood across America. Over 7 million of us currently live with Alzheimer’s — more than 1 million in our two states alone — a number that is expected to nearly double in the decades ahead. Changing the trajectory of Alzheimer’s in America isn’t a luxury — it’s a necessity.

Alzheimer’s can start more than a decade before memory loss and other signs become evident. Early detection is critical to helping patients start Alzheimer’s treatment sooner, when it’s most effective . Sadly, many patients are diagnosed too late for treatment or other health interventions to help.

Thankfully, decades of investment in research and development have led to scientific breakthroughs that are revolutionizing Alzheimer’s care. For too long, diagnosing Alzheimer’s required lengthy referrals and invasive, expensive procedures. Today, simple blood-based biomarker tests can help identify the disease earlier and more conveniently than ever. These developments have the potential to transform patient care, particularly with more treatments now approved.

Yet despite these advances, coverage policies have not kept pace. Medicare can only cover preventive services that Congress has specifically authorized or that are recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. This process can delay coverage for years after screening tests receive FDA clearance.

That’s why we came together to introduce the ASAP Act. Our bipartisan, bicameral legislation authorizes the secretary of Health and Human Services to provide a pathway for Medicare coverage for FDA-approved or cleared blood-based biomarker tests for the early detection of Alzheimer’s and other dementias.

Broadening access to Alzheimer’s screening tools can help people understand their risk for the disease long before symptoms appear. This is especially key for patients in rural and underserved communities, where access to specialists and advanced diagnostic facilities can be limited and where a simple blood test could reduce the burden of traveling long distances for care.

Catching Alzheimer’s early is critical because it is among the most expensive diseases to manage . Late-stage care often requires extensive medical services and long-term support, imposing significant costs to families and taxpayers alike. It can also place an enormous burden on caregivers, who often shoulder years of financial, emotional and logistical responsibilities as a loved one’s condition progresses. Earlier detection can give families more time to plan, pursue treatment and prepare for the challenges ahead.

As our country’s population ages, rates of Alzheimer’s will rise. In fact, the U.S. is on pace to spend more than $1 trillion treating Alzheimer’s and other dementias by 2050. The cost of inaction is exorbitant.

It’s fair to debate whether Medicare should cover new services, but modern blood tests are much softer on taxpayers than a typical PET scan . Yet despite their cost-effectiveness, blood tests can still be financially challenging for the average patient to obtain. By significantly easing out-of-pocket costs, the ASAP Act helps fix this problem.

The legislation reflects principles that both parties can get behind. It encourages prevention, innovation, patient choice and fiscal responsibility — values Republicans have long championed. By increasing access to quality medical care, the ASAP Act advances a more equitable healthcare system where a person’s ability to benefit from the latest innovation isn’t determined by their income status or where they live — a key priority for Democrats.

Ultimately, scientific advancements achieve their full potential only when people can access them. In 1990, Congress voted to ensure Medicare coverage of mammograms , saving the lives of millions of women through early detection and treatment of breast cancer. Today, we have the chance to change Alzheimer’s trajectory and write a new story.

Families deserve access to earlier diagnosis and treatment without being forced to pay out of pocket just to get care. FDA-cleared Alzheimer’s tests are now available; coverage rules need to keep up. Every month we delay costs Americans opportunities to benefit from advances that could make a meaningful difference in their lives.

Two hundred twenty-four of our House colleagues have co-sponsored our bill, a sign of momentum we should not squander. The time for waiting is over. We must act ASAP.

Vern Buchanan serves Florida’s 16th District. He is vice chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, chairman of its Health Subcommittee, and the longest-serving Republican to represent Southwest Florida in the U.S. House of Representatives. Paul Tonko serves New York’s 20th District. He is a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee and serves as ranking member of its Environment Subcommittee.

articles.title: Trump administration brings fight over political ad rates back to Supreme Court
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Thursday urged the Supreme Court to chastise a lower court for intervening — again — in a legal fight between the two major political parties over who can access cheaper television advertising rates in the lead-up to an election. The Supreme Court sided with the GOP last month, ruling that Democrats…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Thursday urged the Supreme Court to chastise a lower court for intervening — again — in a legal fight between the two major political parties over who can access cheaper television advertising rates in the lead-up to an election.

The Supreme Court sided with the GOP last month , ruling that Democrats went to court too early and needed to wait for the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to review their arguments.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit has warned the FCC is now “dragging its feet” to avoid judicial review as November’s contests approach. The judges ordered the FCC to respond to Democrats’ arguments by noon EDT Friday so things can move forward.

“In sum, just as the Fourth Circuit seriously erred when it first tried to leap-frog the Commission’s decision, it has now seriously erred in trying to short-circuit the Commission’s deliberations,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the Supreme Court.

Sauer asked for an immediate intervention ahead of the Friday deadline. He wants the justices to make clear to the 4th Circuit they can’t compel the FCC to act and shouldn’t intervene on the issue again ahead of the midterms.

Republican Party committees quickly backed Sauer’s ask.

“If the case for a stay was strong the first time around, it’s open and shut now,” they wrote in their own emergency appeal , also filed Thursday.

The request heads to Chief Justice John Roberts, who handles emergency matters arising from the 4th Circuit by default. Though he could ultimately refer it to the full court for a vote, Roberts has authority to immediately step in as a singular justice to block Friday’s deadline.

The legal battle concerns a federal mandate that broadcast stations offer their lowest available advertising rate to campaigns in the 60 days preceding a general election. Everyone agrees candidates get the discount, but whether political parties and joint fundraising committees can, too, has come under question.

Republicans argue yes — hoping it will help them put their cash advantage to better use — while Democrats argue no.

After the 4th Circuit agreed with Democrats at an earlier stage of the case, Republicans brought the case to the Supreme Court’s emergency docket.

Over liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson’s dissent, the majority ruled last month that Democrats couldn’t seek the judiciary’s help until after the FCC resolved their petition seeking review of the ad policy. It meant Republican campaign arms could access the discount in the meantime.

It wasn’t a final decision on the actual legality of the policy, however, and the case headed back to the 4th Circuit for more proceedings. On Wednesday, the 4th Circuit ruled 2-1 that the FCC needed to move along given the fast-approaching elections.

“The FCC’s actions are not only unfortunate — but also an assault on our Constitution’s separation of powers. Put simply, the FCC has thumbed its nose at Congress’s statutory commands and the settled principle of judicial review,” the majority wrote.

articles.title: Letitia James' underdog rival turns AG's own playbook against her with scathing 52-count campaign 'indictment'
articles.summary: Saritha Komatireddy released a 52-count faux indictment against Letitia James, accusing the New York attorney general of neglecting hate crimes and fraud.
articles.body: The Republican challenging New York Attorney General Letitia James released a mock 52-count indictment Thursday, accusing the Democratic incumbent of neglecting her duties as the state’s top law enforcement official. The 52-count mock indictment accuses James of failing to address mentally ill people living on the streets, repeat offenders, hate crimes and fraud while focusing instead on political battles with President Donald Trump. Rather than tackle these issues, GOP candidate Saritha Komatireddy charges that James has been too focused on sparring with President Donald Trump. The attack comes just hours before James and Komatireddy are set to face off Thursday night in their first televised debate of the general election campaign. Komatireddy is a former federal prosecutor who secured convictions against Islamist terrorists and prosecuted Mexican drug cartel leaders. The indictment-style press release appears to turn James' own legal playbook against her, with Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor, casting the attorney general as the defendant. CORNELL SEXUAL ASSAULT CASE REVIVES SCRUTINY OF A LITTLE-KNOWN NEW YORK LAW ON INTOXICATED VICTIMS "When a law keeps prosecutors from charging rape, it is the chief law enforcement officer’s job to get it changed," Komatireddy wrote. "The defendant (James) had eight legislative sessions and a Legislature led by her own party. Beyond one social media post, the People have found no evidence that she made the bill a priority." James’ campaign has dismissed Komatireddy’s messaging as a simple campaign stunt. "Attorney General Letitia James files real lawsuits in real courts every day to protect New Yorkers’ rights and their wallets," a James campaign spokeswoman told Fox News Digital. "While Saritha Komatireddy spent today writing this press release, the attorney general announced the arrest and indictment of a Queens pharmacy owner for defrauding Medicaid to the tune of $31 million." NY AG HOPEFUL BLASTS LETITIA JAMES AS MEDICAID FRAUD RECOVERIES COLLAPSE: 'SHE'S NOT DOING THE JOB' A Komatireddy spokeswoman fired back, arguing that such a charge was rich coming from James. "Tish James is one to talk about campaign stunts! Her entire tenure as attorney general has been one long political campaign stunt," Komatireddy spokeswoman Nicole Kiprilov told Fox News Digital. "While Letitia was busy chasing her next political headline, crime rose 26%, homelessness rose 38%, and New York became the laughingstock of the nation in prosecuting Medicaid fraud — dead last. Those are the real consequences of an Attorney General more interested in political theater than public safety." TRUMP LAWYERS TARGET WHAT LETITIA JAMES WON’T SAY ABOUT EVIDENCE IN $450M CASE New York is a deep blue state, and Komatireddy’s odds of coming out on top in November are slim. A Siena University poll released last month had James leading Komatireddy 52% to 39%. While James' lead is commanding, it’s also shrinking, with her advantage over Komatireddy narrowing by five points between August and September in Siena University's polling. Andrew Cuomo that preceded his resignation.

articles.title: Durbin demands Schmitt records and an apology for Jack Smith
articles.summary: Senate Judiciary Democrats accused their GOP counterparts of violating committee rules by failing to share documents that served as the basis for a confusing flub about sports teams when questioning Jack Smith last week. They’ve also demanded an apology for the former special counsel. Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) has faced backlash after he accused Smith…
articles.body:
Senate Judiciary Democrats accused their GOP counterparts of violating committee rules by failing to share documents that served as the basis for a confusing flub about sports teams when questioning Jack Smith last week. They’ve also demanded an apology for the former special counsel.

Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) has faced backlash after he accused Smith of attending an Atlanta Hawks NBA game, implying he may have met with fellow President Trump prosecutor Fulton County, Ga., District Attorney Fani Willis (D). Smith has denied ever meeting her.

The question befuddled Smith, who later recalled he attended a game between the Iowa Hawkeyes and the Maryland Terrapins around that same time.

The Democrats’ letter, spearheaded by ranking member Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), notes that the majority is required to share records it receives with the minority.

“As of the date of this letter, we still have not received these records. We request that you immediately provide these and all other documents that you have withheld, commit to fully complying with Senate rules in the future, and apologize to Mr. Smith on behalf of the Committee for the unacceptable personal attacks and false accusations of perjury he faced during this hearing,” the letter states.

Durbin called Schmitt’s questioning “an effort to manufacture a connection between Mr. Smith and the Fulton County Georgia District Attorney. The texts established only that Senator Schmitt had not done the basic due diligence of verifying a document before relying on it.”

“Nonetheless, Senator Schmitt incorrectly asserted to Mr. Smith, ‘I think you’ve already perjured yourself,’ and inexcusably branded him ‘a dirtbag,’ language which is beneath the dignity of this Committee and the Senate,” he wrote.

A spokesperson for committee Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), to whom the letter is addressed, rejected the idea, noting the senator’s own recent work investigating Smith, including that he reviewed small dollar donations made to conservative groups.

“It’s Jack Smith who owes an apology to the thousands of Americans he and his staff ran roughshod over,” spokesperson Clare Slattery said in a statement.

The Hill has obtained the messages the committee’s Democrats now seek, which show the limited basis for Schmitt’s line of questioning.

The texts amount to a few exchanges the night of Feb. 3, 2024, and don’t reference a team name at all — instead largely showing prosecutors on Smith’s team coordinating over finding their seats in the area and agreeing to mingle at halftime.

After asking if a seat in row 109 was reserved for Smith, a member of his team asked if there might be room to join them.

“We are in 201. High; but center court. I will swing down at half to say hello,” JP Cooney, Smith’s then-deputy, wrote in the text.

Smith told lawmakers during last week’s hearing that he went to the Maryland game because he was interested in seeing Iowa star player Caitlin Clark.

Though included elsewhere in the documents, there were signs the group was interested in women’s basketball.

In late March 2024 — a few weeks after the prosecutors’ outing — Smith’s staff again discusses basketball, with prosecutor David Harbach writing, “P.s. Caitlin Clark on tonight at 8pm on ESPN.”

Schmitt has said he was largely focused on the timing of the texts, matching that to the tipoff of the Atlanta game. His team also said he did not see the messages about Clark.

“Senator Schmitt has never seen texts referencing Caitlin Clark, hence why he asked what game Jack Smith was at. Had Schmitt received those text messages of course he wouldn’t have asked which game he attended. As the Senator has since said, he learned the one thing he and Jack Smith have in common is they are a fan of college sports,” a spokesperson for the senator said last week.

Durbin credits Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) with pressing Schmitt to again show the text messages he flashed during his questioning of Smith and helping connect the dots that Schmitt had the wrong team.

“This farce culminated in a national embarrassment for the Committee, when, in their eagerness to ambush a witness and manufacture a viral moment, Republican Members violated Senate rules by not sharing committee records with the minority and falsely accused a witness of perjury based on their own misunderstanding of these records,” he wrote.

articles.title: Brown holds 6-point lead over Husted in Ohio Senate race survey
articles.summary: Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is ahead of incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) by 6 points in the race for the latter’s seat, according to a new poll. In the CNN poll, 49 percent of respondents said they were leaning in the direction of Brown if the election occurred that day, while 43 percent said…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is ahead of incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) by 6 points in the race for the latter’s seat, according to a new poll.

In the CNN poll, 49 percent of respondents said they were leaning in the direction of Brown if the election occurred that day, while 43 percent said the same of Husted. Five percent said they weren’t leaning in any direction, 2 percent said they were leaning toward someone else and 1 percent had “no opinion.”

The margin of sampling error for the poll is 4.5 percentage points.

Republicans are facing an uphill battle this election cycle, with issues like the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s slumping approval rating and concerns about the cost of living weighing the party down as the midterms approach. Meanwhile, Democrats have outperformed their GOP opponents in recent polling.

Trump, whose approval rating in the CNN poll of Ohio voters was 36 percent, is set to campaign with Husted in Youngstown next week, marking his second trip to Ohio in a month. Sixty-four percent in the poll disapproved of Trump’s job performance.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s national approval rating was sitting at 37.4 percent Thursday morning, while his disapproval rating was 60.3 percent.

Trump won Ohio in the last three presidential elections , with former President Obama carrying the state in 2008 and 2012.

The CNN poll took place from Sept. 29 to Oct. 5 and featured 760 registered Ohio voters.

articles.title: La UCO investiga un plan de las cloacas del PSOE para causar "daño físico" a la jueza Biedma: "Es un puto grano en el culo"
articles.standfirst: Un informe de la Guardia Civil señala que el entorno de Leire Díez habría contactado con una mujer vinculada al clan de 'Los Rochos' para actuar contra la magistrada que investigó a David Sánchez
articles.summary: Un informe de la Guardia Civil señala que el entorno de Leire Díez habría contactado con una mujer vinculada al clan de 'Los Rochos' para actuar contra la magistrada que investigó a David Sánchez
articles.body: La Unidad Central Operativa (UCO) de la Guardia Civil ha trasladado al juez de la Audiencia Nacional Santiago Pedraz un informe en el que detalla los presuntos contactos del entorno de Leire Díez con personas vinculadas al clan de 'Los Rochos' para actuar contra la jueza Beatriz Biedma, que instruyó la causa contra David Sánchez. El documento, incorporado a la investigación sobre la presunta trama vinculada a Leire Díez, recoge el testimonio de Cintia Rocho Leal, conocida como 'La Celsa', quien aseguró a los agentes que el exmagistrado Luis Sáenz de Tejada contactó con ella para hablarle de Biedma. Según su declaración, se refirió a la jueza como "un puto grano en el culo" y afirmó que "había que eliminarla", añadiendo que "a palos aprende el burro". A partir de este testimonio, la UCO aprecia en la actuación descrita "la intención de causar un daño físico" a la magistrada titular del Juzgado de Instrucción número 3 de Badajoz. El origen de una de las líneas de investigación está en una anotación manuscrita encontrada en una agenda de Leire Díez: "Jueza Badajoz. La celsa. Heroína & Gitano". Tras conocerse públicamente la anotación, Cintia Rocho se identificó como 'La Celsa' y relató ante la UCO los contactos que había mantenido con Sáenz de Tejada. Según su declaración, en diciembre de 2024 inició una conversación a través de Facebook con el exmagistrado, quien le habló de una supuesta "mafia judicial" en Badajoz. Posteriormente, un perfil identificado como "José García Fernández" le habría enviado mensajes de audio en los que planteaba "hacer una limpieza" de los juzgados de Badajoz, propuesta que ella rechazó. La UCO destaca que posteriormente se produjo un cambio de enfoque: la conversación pasó de referirse de forma general a los jueces de Badajoz a centrarse en "una actuación concreta dirigida contra la magistrada". Según los investigadores, este viraje se produjo "a iniciativa del exmagistrado". El informe conecta además el testimonio de Cintia Rocho con el del empresario Joaquín Parra Páez, quien declaró sobre los contactos mantenidos en Badajoz durante las actuaciones destinadas, presuntamente, a intervenir en la causa contra David Sánchez. La UCO sostiene que el exmagistrado Sáenz de Tejada habría sido utilizado para tratar de incidir en el procedimiento judicial que afectaba al hermano del presidente del Gobierno. Entre los elementos analizados figura una nota localizada en un dispositivo del empresario Javier Pérez Dolset en la que se podía leer "Jueza del hermano, choriza sin igual" y "Luis Sáenz de Tejada tiene toda la info". Los investigadores también han analizado la actividad del exjuez en redes sociales. Según el informe, Sáenz de Tejada habría difundido fotografías, rumores y contenidos con perfiles falsos relacionados con Biedma. Entre ellos figuraría una imagen falsa de la magistrada en un coche rodeada de preservativos. Además, habría publicado al menos 52 vídeos en YouTube relacionados con el caso de David Sánchez, de los que 34 se centraban en la jueza Biedma, según la UCO. Los agentes consideran que estas actuaciones podían estar dirigidas a cuestionar públicamente la actuación de los magistrados de Badajoz. El exmagistrado también presentó dos denuncias contra Biedma ante la Fiscalía General del Estado, el 21 de octubre y el 27 de noviembre de 2024. La primera no fue admitida a trámite, mientras que la segunda fue remitida a la Fiscalía Superior de Extremadura para su conocimiento y, en su caso, tramitación. Por su parte, Joaquín Parra aseguró que le constaban seguimientos a Biedma, aunque afirmó no tener conocimiento de que se pretendiera llevar a cabo una agresión física contra ella. La investigación trata ahora de determinar el alcance de los contactos con el entorno de Los Rochos, quién promovió las actuaciones contra la magistrada y qué relación tuvieron con el supuesto intento de interferir en el procedimiento judicial sobre David Sánchez. Los hechos forman parte de una causa todavía en fase de instrucción y las conclusiones de la UCO deberán ser valoradas por el juez.

articles.title: Senate Republicans give it one more last chance
articles.summary: Despite efforts by Senate leadership to pass meaningful legislation before the midterm recess, partisan gridlock resulted in the failure of several key bills, leaving the chamber with little progress beyond minor administrative measures and one bipartisan sports act.
articles.body:
In my previous column , I said it probably didn’t matter that the House recessed for the midterm break two weeks earlier than originally planned. There was not much that could be done in that short time frame to turn around public attitudes toward Congress or its ability to resolve issues like high prices, a war, or government corruption. Besides, I argued, people don’t pay much attention to what legislation Congress enacts unless it directly affects their lives and livelihood.

The Senate, nevertheless, stuck to its guns and stayed working these last two weeks on matters that could potentially produce a favorability bump at the polls.

The Senate’s gambit reminded me of the country song, “Give me just a one more last chance, before you say we’re through.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s (R-S.D.) suggestion box soon filled with ideas from his colleagues on how to retain chamber control.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) urged suspending the federal gas tax to bring down prices at the pump. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) pressed their leadership to cap the cost of insulin at $35 . Other proposals were tossed at the wishing wall in hopes they would stick.

Despite the wealth of ideas, the Senate left town late last week with more of a whimper than a bang. Not surprisingly, at this late hour in the midterm countdown, partisan politics and the Senate’s sclerotic legislative pace came into play, resulting in near-gridlock on the legislative gridiron.

Heading the list of Republican leadership priorities was the Ratepayer Protection Act, introduced by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio). It would require state utility regulators to consider making large data centers pay for their own grid and infrastructure costs instead of sticking consumers with the bill. An identical bill previously passed the House overwhelmingly .

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Shumer (D-N.Y.) called Husted’s bill a “fraud” because it is voluntary and would not affect current consumer energy costs because it would not take effect for two years. Last month, Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) blocked Husted from bringing his bill to the floor by unanimous consent. Heinrich and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) have been negotiating their own tougher data center bill and urged senators to wait until after the elections to compare the alternatives.

Husted is facing a tough reelection challenge from former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who has spent millions on ads attacking Husted for supporting data centers and causing electric bills to spiral by thousands of dollars. Thune blasted his Democratic colleagues for blocking Husted’s permitting reform measure simply to deny Republicans another “win” before the election.

With the demise of the data center bill, the Senate spent much of its time on bills of much less importance that could be passed by unanimous consent. Some of these were the routine re-namings of federal post offices and buildings, or designating commemorative days, weeks and months of interest to individual members.

One that caught my eye, introduced by Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), designated Sept. 25, 2026, as “National Lobster Day.” It had been introduced just a day earlier with lead co-sponsor, Susan Collins, who is in a tight reelection race.

In the midst of this mish-mash of measures, the Senate voted 49-50 on Sept. 24 to defeat a resolution by Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) to end the Iran war. It was a Republican victory but one out of favor with the public.

The only major measure the Senate could agree on before it adjourned was a bipartisan bill, the Protect College Sports Act co-sponsored by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.). The bill passed the Senate, 77-22 . It would codify and revise existing standards regulating such things as athletes’ compensation, transfers, and years in school.

The bill is not exactly a campaign vote grabber. Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), with his sardonic wit, said that while he would support the bill, he “hadn’t met a single person on the campaign trail” who said they lay awake at night worrying about those college football coaches.

The moral of this fortnight frenzy in the Senate is: If you’re looking for a last-minute election elixir to secure your future, do not come knocking on legislative doors for a stay-in-power potion. Chances are your fate will not change. Members will win or lose based on their reputation, character, strength of their opponents, and the economy, and not on the number of bill notches in their belts.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran, culminating as chief of staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of, “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial” (2000), and, “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays” (2018).

articles.title: Congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign signs
articles.summary: A Democratic congressional candidate in Arizona said Wednesday that she was raped by two men while repairing a campaign sign in August, revealing an alleged attack she said she initially kept secret out of shame. Bernadette Greene-Placentia, who is challenging Rep. Abe Hamadeh (R) in Arizona’s 8th Congressional District, said she was attacked and knocked…
articles.body:
A Democratic congressional candidate in Arizona said Wednesday that she was raped by two men while repairing a campaign sign in August, revealing an alleged attack she said she initially kept secret out of shame.

Bernadette Greene-Placentia, who is challenging Rep. Abe Hamadeh (R) in Arizona’s 8th Congressional District, said she was attacked and knocked unconscious in a parking lot northwest of Phoenix in the early morning hours of Aug. 14.

Greene-Placentia told authorities she was walking back to her vehicle after fixing a damaged campaign sign when two men approached her from behind and struck her in the head, according to a police report obtained by MS NOW .

According to the file, the House candidate recalled one of the attackers possibly making a politically charged derogatory remark during the attack, though she later acknowledged that she could not be certain what he said. Authorities have not established whether the alleged assault was politically motivated.

The former longtime haul trucker reported the alleged attack to the Maricopa County sheriff’s office on Aug. 31, more than two weeks after it occurred. She shared her account first with the Phoenix New Times , which published it Wednesday.

Greene-Placentia told the outlet she struggled to process what happened and initially did not want to report it because she was “embarrassed” and wanted to “forget it happened.”

She ultimately decided to speak publicly because she felt remaining silent conflicted with her campaign’s message of standing up for all Arizonans.

“I never imagined I would have to tell this story, but I know I am far from the only woman who has lived through something like this,” she said in a statement. “Too many survivors carry these experiences silently. I am speaking out because I want them to know they are seen, they are heard, and they are not alone.”

“Me coming forward is me taking my power back,” the Democrat said in a separate interview with MS NOW.

She won the Democratic primary in July with more than 65 percent of the vote. She is looking to unseat Hamadeh in a district he won by 13 percentage points in 2024.

The candidate said she has no plans to suspend her campaign but has stopped repairing signs alone late at night, a practice she previously did to avoid Arizona’s intense daytime heat.

“What happened will not silence me,” Greene-Placentia said in a statement. “I’m going to keep showing up, keep fighting for this community, and keep working every day to bring real representation to the people of CD8.”

articles.title: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program, alleging fraud
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s administration is suspending tech giant Microsoft from a program to apply for green cards for workers who come to the U.S. to live and work using an H-1B visa as it accuses the company of fraud.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s administration is suspending tech giant Microsoft from a program to apply for green cards for workers who come to the U.S. to live and work using H-1B visas as it accuses the company of fraud. Supporters of the Republican president have long argued that various programs like the one Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing essentially empower American companies to recruit foreign workers for jobs that end up undercutting Americans. In a wide-ranging announcement Thursday, Vance and other top administration officials also called out universities over their use of J-1 visas for international students and information technology outsourcing firms. The announcement came hours before Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, part of an event at which he is granting some of the nation’s most prestigious science and technology awards to his tech billionaire allies. Vance said that the program from which Microsoft is being suspended requires companies to advertise jobs in America before applying to the Department of Labor to show they need to give a foreign worker a green card because of a lack of American workers. “They’ll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They’ll go out there and say that ‘We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.’ And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft.” Vance said Microsoft last year laid off 6,000 American workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said in a White House news conference announcing the decision. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.” Microsoft, which is based in Redmond, Washington, near Seattle, said in a statement that “the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans.” “We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information,” the statement continued, adding that 80% the 6,000 H-1B visa applications it submitted in the last fiscal year, were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees, not to hire new personnel. The remaining filings for new employees were for people “already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country,” it said. Vance said H-1B workers are effectively foreign indentured servants because if they lose their job, they have to leave the country, and they earn less than Americans in the same position. The H-1B program has long been a target of Trump supporters who say that the program undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse. H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find American workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India. The Vance announcement came a day after Trump’s administration launched another broadside against international students and their ability to work in the U.S. The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States. The proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the Optional Practical Training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school. Vance also called out universities that he suggested were abusing a program to allow international students to come to the U.S. These temporary visas, called J-1 visas, allow international visitors to temporarily come to the U.S. for work and study exchange programs. Vance singled out nine universities that he said merited further investigation for J-1 visa fraud, saying they used the program in greater proportions than their counterparts. The universities were Harvard; Yale; Stanford; Brown; the University of Pittsburgh; the University of California, Davis; the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech; Arizona State; and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, or MIT. The universities did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
