articles.title: Keeping Haitians helps America
articles.summary: The administration’s decision to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians threatens to drive skilled workers toward economic competitors like Canada, prompting calls for a bipartisan legislative solution to protect American communities and industries.
articles.body:
As the administration looks to outcompete countries such as Canada, a new approach toward one group of immigrants offers the opportunity for an easy win — including for American businesses and communities.

The administration recently ended Temporary Protected Status for hundreds of thousands of Haitians, many of whom had been lawfully working and contributing before their work authorization ended alongside their protections from deportation.

Many are looking north for refuge and opportunity — to Canada. Haitians who make it there, or to other countries, leave the U.S. with the skills and knowledge they gained here and that are critical to our workforce, especially in sectors such as health care and senior care .

The loss of these workers already hurts, especially in states with large populations of Haitians who had temporary status — with Florida at the top of the list by far. That some would take their talents to our economic competitors compounds the pain.

We’re not saying that Temporary Protected Status should be permanent. But abrupt ends to it, such as for Haitians, underscore the need for an immigration solution for individuals who have built their lives in the U.S., and for the employers and communities who depend on them.

Just ask Republican Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who has said repeatedly that ending protections for Haitians would hurt his state and especially the city of Springfield, where many Haitians live. Detaining and deporting Haitians would be “a blow to Springfield” and “a blow to the state of Ohio,” he said in July .

“These are people who have helped Springfield really come back,” DeWine said. “The Haitians who are living there and [are] employed there, they came there to work, and they came there because there were jobs that were not being filled by other people.”

DeWine also cited the dangerous situation in Haiti — a point faith leaders in Ohio , as well as Florida , Maryland and elsewhere , have made in urging a compassionate solution for Haitian former TPS recipients.

DeWine also predicted that many Haitians would flee to other countries to avoid returning to Haiti, and many Haitians have said as much. In the words of Evka from Florida , “[To] be pulled away to a place that has no safety or security? ‘Scary’ doesn’t even encompass what goes through my mind right now.”

But we don’t have to push Haitians to seek safety elsewhere and give our competitors an economic advantage. Instead, Republicans and Democrats should work together on a solution that allows longtime contributors to remain in the United States.

A bipartisan bill the U.S. House passed in April would be a short-term solution. Recognizing the dire conditions in Haiti, it essentially would restore TPS for Haitians.

A longer-term solution will stabilize communities, meet America’s economic needs and respect human dignity. It will put the U.S. — not our competitors — first.

Jennie Murray is president and CEO of the Forum .

articles.title: US deportations to African countries unlawful and exploit suffering - HRW
articles.summary: More than 500 migrants have been expelled from the US to African countries, HRW says, citing US data.
articles.body:
Campaign group Human Rights Watch (HRW) says the deportation of migrants from the US to third-party African countries is against the law and exploits suffering to deter migration.

"Many, if not most" of the deportees have no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there, HRW says in a report.

Since Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, more than 500 people have been sent to African countries where they are not citizens, the group says, citing US data.

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said "third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets".

Tackling immigration was one of Trump's key pledges during the 2024 election.

Eswatini, which welcomed 32 deportees from the US, says three people - from Yemen, Belize and Laos - "voluntarily departed" to their home countries recently.

According to HRW, some of the countries accepting the deportees have "arbitrarily detained" or sent them to their home countries, where they face "the risk of persecution or torture".

The group said that people sent to Eswatini, Ghana and South Sudan, had been arbitrarily detained and faced ill-treatment while in detention.

In Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and Ghana, the deportees had been sent to their countries of origin despite the risk of "violating the principle of nonrefoulement [that people should not be sent to a country where they face torture, cruel treatment, or threats to their life and freedom]", it said.

The group cited an unnamed US official as having told a Senate hearing that the point for the administration was that it could "threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere".

"The point is to scare people," HRW said.

"Deporting people to countries where they have never set foot is part of a US policy designed to cause human suffering as a means to deter migration," said Michael Garcia Bochenek, the group's interim US programme director.

In a statement from to the BBC, DHS said: "ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe. When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them."

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told the BBC that those being sent to third countries were those whose home nations refused to take them or who had court orders preventing them being sent home.

"Any illegal alien who wants to go home, we will arrange a free flight for them and give them a $3,000 check," she said.

None of the African countries named has commented on the report.

Deported from the US to Ghana then 'dumped' at the border: Nigerian man speaks out

However, while announcing the recent departure of three migrants on Wednesday, Eswatini said that it was committed to ensuring that the "rights, dignity and well-being of third-country nationals were respected and protected".

HRW said it interviewed 24 third-country nationals in six countries - Cameroon, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini and South Sudan.

Some described to the group "abusive treatment" during their deportation flights, including being chained for about 18 hours and with no knowledge of their destination. They were also "denied access to essential medication, and often did not receive sufficient food or water".

"The opaque deals that facilitate these transfers, some of which are still secret, are part of a US policy that violates international human rights law," HRW says.

According to the report, at least a dozen people who identified as lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender (LGBT) were sent to African states that criminalise same-sex relations.

Among them were refugees granted protection in the US based on the likelihood they would be persecuted back home because of their orientation or gender identity.

In November, a Nigerian man deported from the US initially to Ghana expressed his fears to the BBC after he and five others were secretly transferred to Togo.

He spoke of his fears about returning to Nigeria, where his association with a separatist activist group could lead to his arrest and torture.

In DR Congo, HRW says it was told by a US lawyer that of the 15 people from Colombia, Peru and Ecuador deported to the country in April, none remained there by late September, with 11 having returned to their home countries.

"The uncertainty and other conditions they faced in the Democratic Republic of Congo call into question whether these returns to countries of origin were voluntary," the group said.

Equatorial Guinea, which received 65 people, quickly sent at least two people to their home countries, HRW said.

Burundi announced late last month that it had agreed to take in migrants deported from the US.

'We can't do without these people': Trump's migrant crackdown has businesses worried

articles.title: A check is not a plan for improving the FAA
articles.summary: Former FAA air traffic controller Vincent E. Bianco III argued that Congress should approve Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s $30 billion modernization request only if it includes strict conditions like redundant physical routes, milestone-based funding, and integrated staff training.
articles.body:
On Sept. 21, an aging circuit feeding the FAA’s Philadelphia approach control, or TRACON, failed . The system switched to its backup and found the fiber cut. A construction crew in New Jersey had dug it up. Five major Northeast airports went into ground stops: Newark, Teterboro, Philadelphia, LaGuardia and Kennedy.

In an Oct. 1 op-ed, Jackson Shedelbower called that day “another reminder” of why Congress should grant Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s $30 billion request. I spent 23 years in FAA air traffic control as a controller, quality assurance and training specialist, front-line manager and air traffic manager. Nobody wants this system modernized more than the people who have worked it. But his argument reads the lesson backward.

Start with what he gets right. The equipment is old. The circuit that failed was slated for replacement. Controllers and technicians keep this system running with skill and stubbornness, and they deserve better tools. Congress should pay for them. The controllers’ union backs the request , and so do the airlines and the pilots.

Now his own evidence. He reports that roughly two-thirds of the old copper has been replaced with fiber or wireless links. The meltdown happened anyway, and the line the crew cut was fiber. A backhoe does not care whether the cable it cuts is copper or glass.

He also says what the next money buys: “a modern air traffic flow management system and AI-powered software.” Neither is a second route into a control facility.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said as much that day . The agency is laying fiber, he said, but it is “the same data architecture that we’ve had for 50 years.” He wants money to replace it. But the head of the FAA is telling you the problem is design.

Resilience comes from separate physical routes, backups that are tested under load and systems that degrade gracefully when a piece drops out. Money pays for them. Money does not make them.

We have run this experiment. After the Newark outages in the spring of 2025 , the FAA laid new fiber between New York and Philadelphia and said the upgrade put the link on “two separate communications paths” so equipment would keep working “if one path is disrupted.” Sixteen months after those outages, Philadelphia TRACON lost one circuit, found the other cut and took down the Northeast. I cannot tell you those were the same lines. It was the same facility.

We have also run it at scale. NextGen launched in 2003 with the same promises. Last fall the Transportation Department’s inspector general closed the books on it : a program projected at $36 billion between the FAA and the airlines, more than $15 billion of FAA money spent, and about 16 percent of expected benefits delivered. The memo’s causes: no firm requirements, overambitious plans and programs that depended on each other and on airlines buying equipment on schedule.

The current effort shows the pattern. Congress provided $12.5 billion in July 2025 . Bedford told Congress last month that phase one is costing $16 billion. The new request would bring the total to $42.5 billion, against the $31.5 billion the department named last year. The Government Accountability Office found the FAA’s phase one figure leaves out government costs, most operations costs and all of phase two.

Only about a third of the new $30 billion is for air traffic control architecture and software. The rest is split between towers, runways and taxiways, and improvements at midsize airports. None of that two-thirds touches what failed.

Then there are the people who rarely appear in these funding appeals. Controllers must be trained on each new system while still working the traffic. Technicians must maintain old and new side by side until the cutover is finished. I ran a facility training program for nine years. Transition is where the risk lives, and new automation adds workload before it removes any.

Phase one is due by December 2028 . The GAO found the FAA running 11,389 separate project schedules with no master schedule, generally without adjusting them to reduce the load on controllers. A cutover run that way is not modernization. It is a new hazard.

So fund it, with conditions. Require that no critical facility depend on a single physical route, and prove it by test. Release the money against milestones, with the inspector general and GAO reporting before each tranche. Put controller training and technician staffing in the same bill as the hardware. And demand a full lifecycle cost before the vote, not after. Shedelbower himself writes of “necessary investment and oversight.” He argues for the first. This is the second.

Shedelbower asks whether travelers are sick of delays and tells them, “This is the answer.” Money is an ingredient. The answer is a plan that can survive a backhoe.

Vincent E. Bianco III is principal consultant of Marivin Consulting Services LLC. He served 23 years in FAA air traffic control as a controller, quality assurance and training specialist, front-line manager and air traffic manager.

articles.title: Trump administration accuses Maduro of torture in latest indictment
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Thursday unveiled new charges against deposed Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, accusing the duo of ordering physical and psychological torture against Americans and others. According to the superseding indictment, Maduro “presided over this system of repression and torture” while his wife Cilia Flores “ordered that individuals be tortured to…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Thursday unveiled new charges against deposed Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, accusing the duo of ordering physical and psychological torture against Americans and others.

According to the superseding indictment, Maduro “presided over this system of repression and torture” while his wife Cilia Flores “ordered that individuals be tortured to protect her family members’ illegal activity.”

The two have already pleaded not guilty in earlier charges levied after the Trump administration raided Maduro’s home, captured the leader and brought him to the United States, and accused him of narco-terrorism and cocaine trafficking. Asserting that thousands of Venezuelans were “harassed, threatened, arrested, prosecuted, assaulted, tortured, or killed” by people acting at the behest of Maduro’s government, the indictment alleges that the abuse included electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation.

Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on torture methods, sought and got updates on specific victims’ treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner’s child “as a form of psychological torture.”

Maduro is accused of ordering torture as early as 2006, with the indictment saying he and his wife “used military officials assigned to their protective details to torture and intimidate individuals viewed as disloyal or a threat to their illegal narcotics activity.”

“When MADURO MOROS became President of Venezuela in or about 2013, he authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention, and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition.”

Barry Pollock, an attorney for Maduro, pushed back on the allegations in the indictment.

“President Maduro denies the charges in the new indictment and looks forward to his day in court,” he said in a statement.

Thursday’s indictment is the fourth based on charges first brought while Maduro was still in power under the first Trump administration.

The indictment released the January morning after Maduro’s capture laid out 39 counts and accused Maduro of having connections to drug trafficking gangs far beyond the border of Venezuela.

Though that indictment alleges Maduro is connected to six different gangs, details on Maduro’s alleged coordination with them were slim and, in some cases, the indictment included only passing references to the groups.

articles.title: How Elon Musk got back in Trump's orbit after nuclear fallout, insiders reveal: 'Water under the bridge'
articles.summary: Elon Musk is set to receive the National Medal of Science from Trump after their bitter 2025 feud over government spending and DOGE's mission.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: As Elon Musk prepares to receive a prestigious honor from President Donald Trump Thursday afternoon, several sources familiar with the pair's relationship say the trillionaire is back in the administration's fold after last year's nasty blowup between the pair. "Water under the bridge," one former administration official told Fox News Digital when about to classify the falling out and subsequent rekindling of the pair's relationship. Musk had a meteoric rise within the MAGA movement during the 2024 presidential election and, after Trump was re-elected, joined the administration to lead massive federal government cuts under the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). During that time, he had a chummy relationship with Trump, who presented him with a ceremonial golden key to the White House during an Oval Office celebration. In May 2025, Musk left the government after leading DOGE for four months. The CEO of Tesla, SpaceX and X (formerly Twitter) was reportedly at odds with Trump over the amount of government spending tied to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which he viewed as antithetical to DOGE's effort to reduce wasteful spending in a bloated federal government. NEW BOOK ON ELON MUSK EXAMINES THE BILLIONAIRE’S MIND, MOTIVATION AND MAKING LIFE MULTI-PLANETARY On June 3, 2025, Musk took to the social media platform he owns to rail against the bill, describing it as a "disgusting abomination." "KILL THE BILL," Musk wrote on X the following day. Trump fired back in a social media post of his own, saying Musk had been "wearing thin" on him, and that Musk went "CRAZY" after Trump rolled back what the administration described as a Biden-era "backdoor electric vehicle mandate." Musk then claimed that Trump would not have won the 2024 election without his financial support and accused him of "ingratitude." Through his America PAC, Musk helped fund the campaigns of Trump and other Republicans to the tune of nearly $300 million. Musk later accused Trump of being in the infamous Epstein files, though he never provided proof for the claim. TRUMP SAYS MICHAEL COHEN WAS 'WEAPONIZED' BY MAINSTREAM MEDIA IN SURPRISE RADIO REUNION At that point, a former White House official told Fox News Digital that Musk was completely removed from the White House fold. "He wasn’t in the office at all," the source said. Musk had previously occupied a space in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, alongside other White House staff. But, the former official said it's in Trump's nature to rekindle old relationships, regardless of how nasty the dustup. In fact, Trump and his longtime personal attorney, Michael Cohen, just revived their old friendship in September, despite a major falling out and Cohen's testimony against Trump during the 2024 "hush money" trial involving adult entertainer Stormy Daniels. A third source familiar with the matter said Musk began getting back into Trump's good graces earlier this year, while a current administration official disputed the characterization that Musk was fully out of the White House fold in the first place. The administration official said that despite the fallout, Musk has been seen recently at the White House, in part because he's making good on promises to financially support Republican candidates in the 2026 midterm elections. WHAT'S ON THE MENU FOR TRUMP'S STATE DINNER WITH CHINA'S XI? ONE AMERICAN STAPLE IS NOTABLY MISSING Musk has made several high-profile appearances at the White House in recent weeks. He was at the America.gov launch in late September, alongside engineers from the National Design Studio who built the AI-powered website. He appeared again during Trump's state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping last month, and was seated at the president's table. Thursday afternoon, Trump is slated to award Musk the National Medal of Science, the nation's top award for scientific and technological achievement, as first reported by Fox News Digital. "The Trump administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology. These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation," White House spokesperson Liz Huston told Fox News Digital regarding the award. articles.body:
An award-winning filmmaker from Kashmir who legally entered the U.S. and sought asylum has been detained by federal immigration officials, according to his family and supporters .

Arfat Sheikh was arrested Sept. 24 at Washington Dulles International Airport after arriving on a flight from California, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed.

The agency said in a statement that Sheikh “legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance,” adding that a pending immigration application does not automatically grant legal status.

Sheikh moved to the U.S. in 2019 on a student visa to pursue a graduate degree in film at Georgia State University, according to his family. He applied for asylum the following year and had been living in Alexandria, Va.

His family maintains that he was authorized to live and work in the U.S. while his immigration case remained pending.

In August, the Trump administration announced it was working to identify and revoke the visas of more than 200,000 foreign nationals who entered the country on short-term visas and are currently seeking asylum to stay permanently.

Sheikh is best known for 2024 debut feature film, “Saffron Kingdom,” which examines the decades-long conflict in Kashmir through the experiences of members of a family whose journey takes them from Srinagar in the 1990s to Atlanta in 2019.

The film received several awards and accolades, including best feature film honors at the Chicago Filmmaker Awards, the LA Film and Documentary Awards, the Melbourne Independent Filmmakers Festival and the Wake Forest Film Festival.

Sheikh also received the emerging filmmaker activist award at the Teaneck International Film Festival.

His work has focused on Kashmir, a disputed Himalayan region claimed by both India and Pakistan. The two countries each administer portions of the territory and have fought in multiple conflicts over it.

Sheikh is in an immigration detention center, and his family and supporters are raising funds to help secure his release on bond and to cover his legal costs.

articles.body:
It’s Thursday, and #ThankfulThursday is trending on X. Isn’t that nice? We’re thankful you opened 12:30 Report.

Programming note : We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker , filling in for Cate today. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cleibowitz@thehill.com or awalker@thehill.com .

Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed are facing off in their first Senate debate Thursday night.

The tightly contested race has shined a spotlight on Michigan, which President Trump won in 2024, and former President Biden took in 2020.

This is not the first planned debate between the two. They were set to face off last month, but Rogers skipped out because he said the moderator showed “favoritism” toward his Democratic opponent.

Talking points: Rogers, who has championed most of Trump’s policies on the campaign trail, broke with the president on Wednesday after calling for an end to the U.S.’s trade war with Canada.

Tonight, he will likely have to defend his stance, in addition to the war in Iran and affordability. The GOP is navigating a difficult midterm landscape, especially as Trump’s approval rating continues to plummet.

El-Sayed, who beat the more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in the Democratic primary, will likely field debate questions that focus on his more leftist policies, including past calls to defund the police and connections to left-wing streamer Hasan Piker.

Big figures in the fray: Trump called El-Sayed “terrible” and said he “goes back to the days of the Jihad” on Truth Social on Wednesday. He also said Rogers is an “extremely good candidate.”

El-Sayed has been endorsed by former Vice President Harris, who campaigned alongside him last month. And former President Obama is set to rally with him later this month.

What, when, where: Rogers and El-Sayed are facing off in Grand Rapids. The debate will be televised at 7 p.m. EDT by WOOD TV8, a news station owned by The Hill’s parent company, Nexstar Media.

Scott Tranter, Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) director of data science, on Sunday said that “time is running out” for Rogers to close the gap between him and El-Sayed. DDHQ’s forecast shows the Democrat with a 67 percent probability of winning in November, while the Republican holds a 33 percent chance.

During a rally in San Antonio on Wednesday, Trump defended his remarks from earlier this week, when he suggested that Iran could “hit” San Diego and Los Angeles.

“You want to see trauma? You want to see problems? And I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. You want to see a horror show? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles,” the president said to a crowd of supporters.

“You want to see some bad things happen? You want see a country in free fall? We’re not going to let that happen,” he added.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), in response to Trump’s original comments, which he made at a Nebraska rally on Tuesday, told The Hill that the president was “mentally ill” and encouraged lawmakers to invoke the 25th Amendment.

Trump administration pushes back: White House communications director Steven Cheung wrote on X , “The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality.”

He added that Trump was “clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped.”

Another rally incident: The president also accused protesters at the event, held to encourage support for GOP Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton , of being “paid by enemies of our nation.”

The Hill’s Ryan Mancini wrote , “More protesters heckled, with at least one approaching the podium. Rally attendees pushed some of the demonstrators out, with Trump joining in to mock them. He at one point said the protesters ‘are really bad-looking people.’”

Trump will award Elon Musk , and other big leaders in the tech industry, the National Medal of Science on Thursday, according to NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner.

The White House’s “ Science: A New Golden Age ” summit will also present prizes to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , Google co-founder Sergey Brin and founder and CEO of Dell Technologies Michael Dell .

“The Trump Administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology,” Liz Huston , assistant White House press secretary, said in a statement about the event. “These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation.”

According to a bombshell report from The Wall Street Journal, prior to her confirmation, Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay off a $100,000 credit card bill.

The Journal says it reviewed text messages between Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to Donald Trump Jr., and former congressional candidate Eric Deters .

“It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express that’s all it will show. Please,” the texts read.

Three days before her confirmation, Guilfoyle again asked Deters, according to the Journal, writing, “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.”

Rubio’s take: When asked about the report , Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things.”

Another report from the Journal published Tuesday painted an unsavory picture of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and alleged that he contributed to a contentious workplace environment, leading to the departure of a few key officials.

During a Wednesday interview with Fox News’s Lauren Ingraham, Bessent pushed back .

“You’ve apparently made the Wall Street Journal very angry. A piece today read like a TMZ article. Apparently, you have very high standards for your staff. They’re saying that you’re tough on your staff. Have you ever thrown a binder at a wall, Mr. Secretary?” Ingraham asked.

“Look, the Wall Street Journal is a shadow of its former self, and I think it’s a disgrace for you to say that they’re like TMZ. TMZ does a good job of what they do,” Bessent replied.

Bessent further criticized the reporting, telling Ingraham, “There were two — the disgruntled employees … versus, like, the 28 who told them that I’m a great employer, and we have some great employees that come to work every day, just like the American people, and they want to work hard.”

Senate Judiciary Democrats called out their GOP counterparts and demanded they apologize to former special counsel Jack Smith after a hearing flub last week. Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) accused him of attending an Atlanta Hawks NBA game, implying that he may have met with fellow Trump prosecutor Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis (D), whom Smith has denied meeting.

Democrat Bernadette Greene-Placentia , who is challenging Rep. Abraham Hamadeh (R) in Arizona’s 8th Congressional District, said she was raped by two men while repairing a campaign sign in August.

Oil prices are up Thursday amid reports that the White House is weighing strikes on Iran.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Thursday denounced President Trump’s latest attack on Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as “bigoted bulls‑‑‑.”

Schumer wrote on social platform X , “Abdul El-Sayed is on the road to being the next Senator from Michigan no matter how much bigoted bulls‑‑‑ a weak and desperate Donald Trump throws at him.”

Late Wednesday evening, Trump blasted El-Sayed as a “terrible” candidate whose views “are not exactly those of Michiganders” or Americans.

“Mohammed El-Sayed is a terrible Candidate for the Dumocrats,” Trump wrote on Truth Social , using his nickname for Democrats. El-Sayed’s full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.

The president also wrote that El-Sayed, who is Muslim, is a “RADICAL Extremist” and a “Terrorist Sympathizer.”

The Democratic Senate nominee, who is facing off against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in the race to succeed Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.), was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrants.

El-Sayed fired back at the president on Thursday, saying Trump “knows my name is Abdul.”

The Democrat wrote on X , “He says it everyday. But he’s not just attacking me. He’s attacking all of us. He thinks so low of us.

“He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office. He thinks we don’t know any better.”

Trump has frequently gone after the progressive El-Sayed since he defeated Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in the August Democratic primary , using the Senate hopeful’s Muslim faith to cast him as extreme.

In August, Trump posted a split screen of himself and first lady Melania Trump alongside El-Sayed and his wife, Dr. Sarah Jukaku, who is wearing a hijab.

“Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s,” the caption of the split screen stated.

El-Sayed earlier this week challenged the president to campaign for Rogers in Michigan, saying the Republican nominee “can’t speak for” himself.

“Clearly, you are the answer, and you should tell everybody why they should imagine you on the ballot,” the Democrat told MS NOW’s “All In,” directing his remarks at the president.

Decision Desk HQ , a partner of The Hill, gives El-Sayed a 69 percent chance to defeat Rogers. Early voting has already started in some communities and will be available statewide starting Oct. 24.

articles.title: Judge extends temporary block on Trump’s media ban
articles.summary: A federal judge on Thursday briefly extended an order lifting a ban implemented by the White House last month on three new outlets President Trump said should not be allowed to cover him over what he has called “fake news” that puts national security in danger. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, is weighing whether…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Thursday briefly extended an order lifting a ban implemented by the White House last month on three new outlets President Trump said should not be allowed to cover him over what he has called “fake news” that puts national security in danger.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, is weighing whether to issue a longer-lasting injunction after he handed down a 14-day temporary restraining order last month that required the administration to immediately restore press credentials for reporters from CNN, Politico and MS NOW.

That order was set to expire at 11:59 p.m. EDT Thursday, but Kelly said at the start of the hearing that it would be in effect for “another two business days.”

The administration has advanced a familiar argument to justify the president’s decision to restrict media access to his administration, citing national security concerns and the use of anonymous sources.

The news outlets have insisted Trump’s initial comments that the ban was based on cumulative negative coverage are evidence of viewpoint discrimination by the government, which is prohibited under the First Amendment.

Ted Boutrous, a lawyer representing the media outlets, specifically pointed to a recent Time magazine interview in which Trump railed against their coverage as a “confession” of the president’s intent.

The judge did not address the First Amendment claims in his previous order, instead finding that the ban likely violated the media organizations’ constitutional due process rights. The White House sent letters to each outlet identifying stories that it says “threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods,” but those only came after the fact.

Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik argued those letters satisfied the notice requirement, even if the outlets opted not to respond, which happened in this case.

The ban has roiled the daily operation of the White House press corps since the president’s social media post announcing his desire to punish the three outlets and has impacted pool coverage of his activities.

CNN and Politico have both been blocked from traveling with Trump on Air Force One on multiple occasions since Kelly’s initial ruling, a move the media outlets’ attorney argues is causing the companies immediate harm and needs to be rectified.

Other broadcast networks temporarily held back on their duties covering the president on their assigned days after CNN was blocked from fulfilling its turn in the pool rotation.

The Justice Department and a number of White House officials have argued the president has the authority to control access to certain restricted spaces, including the presidential jet and the Oval Office, for any reason.

It mirrors an effort by the West Wing to scale back access granted to The Associated Press last year over the wire service’s refusal to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.”

The West Wing has also sought to block Politico from print pool duties on one occasion since the court ordered their access to the White House grounds be reinstated.

A White House official told The Hill this week media outlets are granted access to attend and cover presidential events “unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right.”

articles.body:
Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Thursday that Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and Trump administration consultants Chris LaCivita and James Blair “need to answer a lot of questions” following recent news reports.

On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle asked President Trump donor Eric Deters, the former co-owner of Snappy Tomato Pizza, to wire $100,000 to her American Express account in a way that wouldn’t leave a paper trail.

And The New York Times reported Tuesday that LaCivita and Blair were in the Balkans advising a pro-Russian political party in Republika Srpska, a small self-governing territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and made hundreds of thousands of dollars.

“But Guilfoyle, LaCivita, Blair — they need to answer a lot of questions because, on its face, it’s at best horrible optics, and at worst, something that’s worthy of a termination,” Tillis told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer on “The Situation Room.”

The senator called the report on Guilfoyle “horrible optics” and compared it to the report on LaCivita and Blair.

“From the outside, it looks awful. I’m willing to give them the benefit of the doubt, but those are very clearly legitimate questions that should be asked [by] members of Congress,” Tillis said.

On the latter story, Blitzer asked the North Carolina Republican if Trump should fire the two advisers. Tillis pointed to Srpska’s ties to Russia, which he said is looking to influence elections in Europe as it wages war in Ukraine. He warned that Russia “is playing us like a fiddle in terms of showing any sort of olive branch towards them.”

“I mean, the way that they are trying to spin what they are doing in Ukraine and what [Russian President Vladimir] Putin ultimately wants to do through the whole of that part of Eastern Europe is very concerning to me,” Tillis said. “We should not have any fingerprints in the Republic of Srpska.”

When asked by Blitzer if he would support investigations into alleged abuses of power and corruption in the White House if Democrats reclaim Congress in November, Tillis said he would “if they’re done properly.”

He made similar remarks about LaCivita and Blair Wednesday night, telling CNN’s Kasie Hunt that the two “should get out of that relationship” with Srpska “very, very quickly,” calling a it “destabilizing force.”

Guilfoyle, the ex-wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), was engaged to Donald Trump Jr. until the two broke up in 2024. She worked as a Fox News co-host until 2018.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio while in Greece on Wednesday declined to comment on the Journal report about her. He told reporters that the story had been “literally posted a few hours ago” and that he did not know “if it’s true or not true.”

Trump said he would fire LaCivita and Blair if their work conflicted with the White House, saying the two are “outside consultants.”

“They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C.,” he wrote on Truth Social. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”

articles.title: Bipartisan lawmakers push colleagues to accept midterm results
articles.summary: A bipartisan pair of lawmakers is urging House colleagues to accept the outcome of November’s elections, whichever side wins. The campaign arrives as President Trump and some of his Republican allies are claiming, without evidence, that the elections are “rigged” in favor of Democrats. In a letter still being circulated on Capitol Hill, Reps. Josh…
articles.body:
A bipartisan pair of lawmakers is urging House colleagues to accept the outcome of November’s elections, whichever side wins.

The campaign arrives as President Trump and some of his Republican allies are claiming, without evidence, that the elections are “rigged” in favor of Democrats.

In a letter still being circulated on Capitol Hill, Reps. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.) and Don Bacon (R-Neb.) are fighting to dispel the argument that America’s elections are anything but secure. Gottheimer is running for reelection, and Bacon is retiring, but both are seeking a pledge from lawmakers in both parties to put trust in voters — and the voting system — and embrace the midterm results.

Congress’s oath to defend the Constitution, they note, demands it.

“Through war and peace, through eras of bitter division and moments of national unity, one practice has held constant: those duly elected under the laws of their states take their seats, and the results of a free election are honored regardless of who prevails,” the lawmakers wrote.

“This is among the oldest and most consequential traditions of our nation — the quiet, orderly act by which the consent of the governed becomes the authority to govern.”

Just a few years ago, demanding such a commitment might have been unheard of. But Trump has cast doubt on the integrity of the country’s elections for more than a decade, warning that the system is rife with fraud, illegal ballots and foreign interference — all designed to help Democrats.

Trump has never provided evidence to back those claims, and numerous studies across decades of elections have found election fraud to be exceedingly rare. Still, many of the president’s allies have accepted his false claims at face value — a dynamic that culminated in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, where a violent mob of Trump supporters sought to overturn the 2020 results.

That effort failed, but a majority of House Republicans voted shortly after the attack to reverse the results in Arizona, Pennsylvania or both. Among them was now-Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who had devised a legal rationale for disputing Trump’s defeat. That’s led to some concern among Democrats that House GOP leaders, guided by Trump, will simply refuse to seat incoming Democrats if they win the majority in the midterms.

Heading into the midterms, Trump has adopted similar rhetoric as he has in the past, warning that Democrats can win only by cheating. And top Cabinet officials, including the heads of the departments of Justice and Homeland Security, have suggested they’re ready to send federal agents to monitor the polls in the name of fighting fraud.

The situation has sparked concerns among state election officials in both parties. And it’s alarmed Democrats in the Capitol, who have launched a broad campaign to prepare local election officials and state attorneys general to defy any administrative effort to disrupt voting or corrupt the election results.

Bacon’s decision to join Gottheimer on the new letter is an indication that at least some Republicans are also concerned about partisan interference in the process.

“There has never been a more critical moment to affirm the integrity of the House of Representatives and its foundational role in our nation’s democracy,” Gottheimer and Bacon wrote.

articles.title: Carville asks if Trump is ‘trying to lose’ midterms or if there is ‘some other explanation’
articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville questioned President Trump’s midterms strategy as Republicans face a rocky political road this election cycle. On a Thursday episode of his “Politics War Room” podcast, Carville and co-host Al Hunt discussed Trump’s controversial statements regarding Iran potentially striking Los Angeles and San Diego, prompting the strategist to ask if the president…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist James Carville questioned President Trump’s midterms strategy as Republicans face a rocky political road this election cycle.

On a Thursday episode of his “Politics War Room” podcast, Carville and co-host Al Hunt discussed Trump’s controversial statements regarding Iran potentially striking Los Angeles and San Diego, prompting the strategist to ask if the president “trying to lose.”

“I mean, there’s nothing that he does that’s consistent with trying to win, and [there’s] probably not much he can do. He is the central issue in the campaign, he dominates everything. But I got to keep asking: Is he trying to do this? Does he just want to screw the congressional Republicans? Does he hate them?” Carville said.

He continued, “I don’t know. There’s some other explanation for this behavior. It might be that he’s just out of his goddamn mind. Who knows?”

Republicans are facing an uphill battle in this year’s midterms, campaigning as the Trump administration deals with the Iran war’s increasing unpopularity, the president’s sagging approval numbers and mounting cost of living concerns. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ favors Democrats to win back both chambers of Congress this fall.

According to a Thursday morning DDHQ polling average , Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 37.4 percent.

“One thing I’m not worried about is Donald Trump out there campaigning. He is out of control,” Hunt said before highlighting the president’s comments on the California cities and disputed inflation claims .

In a recent Reuters/Ipsos survey, 51 percent of Trump voters felt enthusiastic, either very or somewhat, to vote next month. By contrast, the enthusiasm rate for those who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris was 15 percentage points higher.

On Saturday, Trump pressed his supporters to go to the polls for next month’s midterms, pledging a “big” GOP victory if they do so.

“You got to get out and vote. You got to get out. You got to vote for these guys,” Trump said during the Ohio rally.

When reached for comment, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement that, “James Carville is a stone-cold loser who suffers from a severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome, and it has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain.”

articles.title: Mamdani doubles down on anti-Israel Oct 7 statement after backlash
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani doubled down on his accusation that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, refusing to walk back remarks that sparked bipartisan backlash.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani doubled down on his October 7 statement accusing Israel of carrying out a "genocide" in Gaza on Thursday. Mamdani made the statement while speaking to the press at an unrelated event on Thursday. Reporters asked him about anger in the Jewish community over his statement on the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 terrorist attacks that briefly recognized that day's atrocities before accusing Israel of carrying out genocide against Palestinians. "Do you believe you made any missteps that inflamed tensions in this very difficult moment for a lot of New Yorkers?" a reporter asked. ISRAEL AMB TORCHES MAMDANI OCT 7 POST: 'LIKE TURNING SEPTEMBER 11 INTO A DAY OF MOURNING FOR AL-QAEDA' "I believe that there must be room to mourn every single life," Mamdani responded. "There must be room to mourn the lives of the more than 1,100 that Hamas killed three years ago; there must be room to mourn the 74,000 Palestinians that the Israeli government has killed since." "There must be room to reckon with the ways in which so many New Yorkers' lives have been shattered," he continued, noting that the vigil he attended highlighted testimonies from those killed "either on the day or the genocide since." WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM Mamdani went on to accuse the Israeli government of using the October 7 massacre as "a justification for a genocide." The mayor also repeatedly declined to say that he would change anything about the statements he made on Wednesday, either in his formal statement or during his attendance at the October 7 vigil. He also justified his greater emphasis on Palestinian deaths, arguing that "this is something that is ongoing, as opposed to something that simply happened three years ago." In his statement on Wednesday, Mamdani condemned Hamas’ attack as a "horrific war crime" while also characterizing Israel’s subsequent military operation as a genocide. NETANYAHU ACCUSES MAMDANI OF 'FOMENTING HATE,' SAYS RHETORIC IS MAKING NEW YORK JEWS AFRAID "The suffering did not begin nor end that day," he wrote. "It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children." Israel has rejected accusations that it is committing genocide in Gaza, saying its military targets Hamas and other terrorist groups while seeking to minimize civilian casualties. The mayor's statement sparked bipartisan backlash, with Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., calling it "egregious and insulting." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There are 364 days of the year to focus on that. This is a day that should just be focused on what was by all agreement a horrific terror attack," Goldman, who is Jewish, told Politico. "What the mayor’s statement did today was to blame Israelis for the attack that they suffered three years ago. Regardless of what you actually think of the conflict and what’s happened either since or before, there’s no excuse for victim blaming."

articles.title: Dem House hopeful alleges she was brutally attacked during 2 am campaign errand
articles.summary: Bernadette Greene-Placentia says she was knocked unconscious and sexually assaulted while repairing her campaign signs in Sun City, Arizona.
articles.body: Arizona Democratic congressional candidate Bernadette Greene-Placentia said she was knocked unconscious and raped during an overnight encounter with two attackers in August while trying to repair a damaged campaign sign. Greene-Placentia told Phoenix New Times that she was walking through a parking lot in Sun City shortly after 2 a.m. on Aug. 14 to repair a damaged campaign sign when someone struck her in the head, knocking her unconscious. Greene-Placentia said she regained consciousness to find a man raping her and kicked at a second man who approached her, according to the Phoenix New Times. A public information officer with the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office confirmed to Fox News Digital that a police report was filed on Aug. 31. SCANDALS, SOCIALISTS AND TRUMP ROIL PRIMARIES, SEND INCUMBENTS PACKING AT NEAR-RECORD PACE "Detectives advised it is still an ongoing investigation, and we cannot comment on the investigation at this time," said the officer. Greene-Placentia initially told investigators that one of her attackers used a derogatory remark she interpreted as "Democratic b----," according to the Phoenix New Times, but told The New York Times on Wednesday that she could not be sure what she had heard. Greene-Placentia told Phoenix New Times she suffered extensive bruising and vaginal bleeding for three days after the alleged assault and believed she may have sustained a concussion. Greene-Placentia missed a campaign event and was out of contact with her staff for about two days following the alleged assault, according to The New York Times. She later told campaign aides and her husband what happened before reporting it to police on Aug. 31, saying she initially felt embarrassed and wanted to forget the incident. She ultimately decided to go public to encourage other sexual assault survivors to speak out. "I never imagined I would have to tell this story, but I know I am far from the only woman who has lived through something like this," Greene-Placentia said in a statement released Wednesday. "Too many survivors carry these experiences silently. I am speaking out because I want them to know they are seen, they are heard and they are not alone." DEMOCRATS TARGETING 12 ADDITIONAL RED DISTRICTS IN MIDTERMS PUSH TO RETAKE HOUSE "What happened will not silence me. I’m going to keep showing up, keep fighting for this community, and keep working every day to bring real representation to the people of CD8," she added. Greene-Placentia received support from both Republicans and Democrats, including her Republican opponent, Rep. Abe Hamadeh, who called for authorities to investigate the alleged attack. "I have read the disturbing story and call upon authorities to investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law. No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community," Hamadeh said in a statement. "This was a cruel and cowardly attack, and it has no place in Arizona. No one should have to fear for their safety, or the safety of the people they love, while serving their community," Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs' office said in a statement to the Phoenix New Times. Fox News Digital reached out to Greene-Placentia's campaign for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hamadeh has represented Arizona's 8th Congressional District since January 2025. Fox News' Power Rankings rate the district as solidly Republican heading into the 2026 midterm elections.

articles.title: Nicolas Maduro and wife Cilia Flores face new charge of conspiracy to torture Americans
articles.summary: Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores face conspiracy to torture charges involving electric shock, asphyxiation and rape of detainees, including U.S. citizens.
articles.body: The U.S, District Court for the Southern District of New York charged former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores with conspiracy to commit torture to Americans and others to stay in power, according to a superseding indictment filed Thursday. Maduro's government, according to the indictment, "presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens." The torture included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture, such as threats to harm and kill victims' families, including children," the indictment read. The charge carries a maximum of life imprisonment if any of the alleged torture resulted in death, and a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison if not. FAMILIES SUE MADURO IN US, ACCUSE EX-PRESIDENT OF DIRECTING POLICE UNIT TIED TO EXTRAJUDICIAL KILLINGS In one incident, the indictment alleges that a U.S. detainee in Venezuela was beaten for days and doused with a noxious liquid that made him vomit, which Venezuelan officers then allegedly made him eat. WAR CRIMES COURT TURNS 'BLIND EYE' TO TOP WORLD THREATS WHILE TARGETING AMERICANS, TRUMP ADMIN ACCUSES The detainee, who was allegedly accused of plotting to kill Maduro, was also subjected to electric shock torture to his torso and genitals and injected with a substance that induced seizures. "On one occasion, CC-3 personally observed Victim-7 being electrocuted; laughed at and taunted Victim-7 during the electric shock; and directed other DGCIM officers in connection with the electric shock," the indictment read. MADURO'S ALLEGED 'BAG MAN' ALEX SAAB ARRESTED LESS THAN 3 YEARS AFTER BIDEN PARDON: REPORT After spending eight-and-a-half months at Boleíta Norte prison in Venezuela, the detainee was released and returned to the U.S. in October 2022, according to the indictment. The indictment alleges Maduro and Flores "inflicted severe physical and mental pain and suffering to repress and punish political opposition, silence dissent and perceived dissent, preserve and protect the power and authority of the members of the conspiracy, and intimidate, harass, and neutralize their opponents, including through kidnappings." The pair, who face numerous other charges, were arrested in Venezuela in January during Operation Absolute Resolve. Maduro was originally charged with narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices, and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices in a 2011 indictment that President Donald Trump's Department of Justice unsealed in 2020. Flores was then charged in a superseding indictment in January with cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices, and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices. They have pleaded not guilty and a trial is scheduled for June 2027. EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY' Flores appeared in court Thursday for a bond hearing on her motion for release from jail. Her lawyers were requesting home confinement with GPS tracking, citing a heart condition and arguing she does not pose a danger to the community. U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied the request. The U.S. government opposes her release, arguing she poses a flight risk and danger to the public. Flores' attorneys say she denies the allegations against her, and both she and Maduro have filed motions to dismiss on diplomatic immunity grounds. articles.title: 5 things to watch for in Thursday’s Michigan debate showdown
articles.summary: Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed will face off Thursday night in their first debate of a contest that will help decide whether Democrats or Republicans hold the Senate majority next year. El-Sayed enjoys a 4.1 percent lead in the Decision Desk HQ polling average heading into the debate. The Cook…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed will face off Thursday night in their first debate of a contest that will help decide whether Democrats or Republicans hold the Senate majority next year.

El-Sayed enjoys a 4.1 percent lead in the Decision Desk HQ polling average heading into the debate. The Cook Political Report lists the race as a toss-up; it’s the only Democratic-held Senate seat rated as a toss-up by the nonpartisan handicapper at this stage.

A Rogers win would make it tougher, though not impossible, for Democrats to take away the Senate majority from Republicans. Democrats must net a total of four seats to win the majority.

El-Sayed won a tough Democratic primary and has been seen as vulnerable by the GOP, but Rogers is facing a difficult election climate for Republicans and has begun to seek distance from the Trump White House on the Iran war and the trade fight with Canada .

WOOD TV8, a Grand Rapids news station owned by The Hill’s parent company, Nexstar Media, will host the debate. The event will air live at 7 p.m. EDT, and each candidate will have a minute to respond to questions and 30 seconds for follow-ups, rebuttals and closing statements.

NewsNation will simulcast the debate, to be moderated by WOOD-TV political reporter Rick Albin and anchor Amber Krycka. NewsNation’s Chief Washington anchor, Leland Vittert, will host the simulcast, while NewsNation and The Hill Politics Editor Chris Stirewalt will provide analysis and a review of the debate at 8 p.m. on CUOMO.

Will either candidate try to appeal to Black voters ?

Black voters are typically a Democratic constituency, but there are reasons to think they could be a vulnerability for El-Sayed.

Black voters largely backed Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in the primary fight. The Hill reported in August that she led El-Sayed by 8 percentage points in districts where more than 15 percent of the population is Black.

Polling in July showed that just 21 percent of Black voters backed El-Sayed while 67 percent supported the House Democrat.

Young voters in general back El-Sayed in polls, but young Black voters who back El-Sayed worry that older Black voters either won’t show up or could vote for Rogers.

During an appearance on NewsNation’s “On Balance” this week, political commentator Adolph Mongo noted that El-Sayed in 2024 encouraged the Arab American community in Michigan to not back former President Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris over the Biden administration’s policies toward Israel, arguing Black voters in the state remember that.

El-Sayed has captured support from some voters who feel they have been forgotten by the political class.

In some ways, it is similar to what President Trump was able to do with the electorate. And Trump has been successful in Michigan, winning the state in 2016 and 2024, while losing it to Biden in the 2020 election.

But Rogers is also running against Trump’s low approval ratings, which have been a drag on GOP candidates in Michigan and in other states.

Can Rogers communicate to poor, mostly educated white voters in Michigan that he understands their pain and is willing to do something about it, and not just defend Trump’s record?

Will El-Sayed seek to assuage voters on Israel and Gaza ?

In an interview Tuesday, El-Sayed called my question about whether Israel or Iran was a bigger danger to America a dumb question.

“I’ve been more than extremely clear on this, I don’t want our tax dollars being used to subsidize war abroad. I don’t want our tax dollars being used to fund unconditionally foreign militaries,” El-Sayed began, before adding that the U.S. should be the “first among equals to enforce international law against any and every country that breaks it.”

“So this sort of, like, hypothetical about who’s a bigger threat is a dumb question, I’m sorry,” El-Sayed said.

The Israel-Hamas war was major issue in the Democratic primary, and El-Sayed’s voice of support for Gaza ending up being the one popular with primary voters.

But there are plenty of voters in the general election who have been worried about some of his comments, and El-Sayed has sought to shift — most notably by apologizing for comments he made following an attack on a Detroit-area synagogue earlier this year.

“I made a mistake,” El-Sayed said during an appearance before the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus at the state party’s convention in August. “I should have issued a statement, of course condemning it, and it just should have been the full stop.”

Will Rogers seek to go on the attack on these issues tonight? And will El-Sayed try to do more to assuage any fears independent or conservative Democratic voters may have of him?

El-Sayed is a generational talent as a communicator, while Rogers in most cable news hits has seemed out of practice.

El-Sayed is definitely going to go after Rogers and prosecute his case. Can Rogers do the same without looking practiced, awkward and consultant-driven?

There will be a third person on the debate stage. His name is Donald Trump.

El-Sayed keeps daring Trump to come to Michigan. When I asked him why he thinks that will be helpful, the Democratic nominee said: “Why do I think that’s going to help me? People hate Donald Trump,” before laughing .

“He wants everyone to know that he’s on the ballot. I want everyone to know that he’s on the ballot, too. Mike Rogers is a vote for Donald Trump. I want him to come and say it for himself. I think he’s too afraid,” El-Sayed said, before arguing that the Rogers campaign likely doesn’t want Trump to come to Michigan.

How does Rogers deal with Trump? Does he get asked, and how does he respond about a Trump visit. And can he make himself his own man?

Also, does El-Sayed look silly trying to run against someone who is not there?

articles.title: Trump to campaign in Alaska amid midterm blitz
articles.summary: President Trump is set to headline a midterm rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Tuesday, just one week after Vice President Vance hit the campaign trail in the state. Former vice presidential nominee and Gov. Sarah Palin (R) served as mayor of the Alaska city from 1996 to 2002. The development comes after Vance campaigned in…
articles.body:
President Trump is set to headline a midterm rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Tuesday, just one week after Vice President Vance hit the campaign trail in the state.

Former vice presidential nominee and Gov. Sarah Palin (R) served as mayor of the Alaska city from 1996 to 2002.

The development comes after Vance campaigned in the state earlier this week, holding a rally in Fairbanks on Monday.

Trump and Vance are hoping to boost the state’s incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), who is facing a competitive reelection bid . Sullivan is running against former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska), as well as another Republican named Dan J. Sullivan.

The race has become increasingly competitive between the incumbent senator and former congresswoman. Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an election handicapper based at the University of Virginia, moved the race from “toss-up” to “leans Democratic” earlier this week.

Decision Desk HQ, another election handicapper, also has Peltola slightly favored to win, while the Cook Political Report has the race in the “toss-up” category.

Trump has sought to boost the incumbent Alaska senator, most recently involving Sullivan in the announcement of a $54 billion investment in a project to export natural gas from the state.

“So, I want to thank, in particular, Dan Sullivan for getting this deal done,” Trump said alongside the lawmaker last week in the Oval Office.

articles.title: GOP donor in Guilfoyle scandal blasts Trump sons, Kushner: ‘I don’t like their yuck-yuck world’
articles.summary: The MAGA donor who Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, reportedly asked for payment ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing expressed frustration Thursday morning with the business dealings of President Trump’s family. The donor, attorney Eric Deters, said Guifoyle asked him to wire $100,000 ahead of the hearing and paid the president’s two oldest…
articles.body:
The MAGA donor who Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, reportedly asked for payment ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing expressed frustration Thursday morning with the business dealings of President Trump’s family.

The donor, attorney Eric Deters, said Guifoyle asked him to wire $100,000 ahead of the hearing and paid the president’s two oldest sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, a total of $300,000 in speaking fees, The Wall Street Journal first reported Wednesday.

Deters told MS NOW’s Peter Alexander that he had “no issues” with these payments but expressed disapproval with their cryptocurrency ventures .

“The only thing that bothers me about [Donald Trump Jr.] and Eric Trump is how they, along with their father, are getting rich out in the open with crypto and everything else,” he said. “President Trump said he hated crypto, his sons get in crypto, now he loves crypto.”

Guilfoyle, California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s (D) ex-wife, was engaged to Trump Jr. until the two broke up in 2024.

Deters also criticized Trump’s son-in-law and political adviser, Jared Kushner, for the controversial $2 billion his private equity firm received from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund after leaving the first Trump administration.

“I’m a Midwest farm boy. I’m a good dude. I don’t like their yuck-yuck world,” the donor said, adding, “You couldn’t pay me to go back to Mar-a-Lago.”

Deters, who also contributed $125,000 to the PAC supporting Trump in 2022, has unsuccessfully run for Congress and Kentucky governor.

The Journal reported Wednesday that Guilfoyle pleaded with Deters to send funds to her American Express account ahead of her July 9 confirmation hearing. He did not ultimately send the money and told her it would cause problems in his marriage.

The GOP donor slammed the U.S. ambassador as “wicked, evil person” and a “grifter” during his interview with MS NOW.

“Kimberly Guilfoyle , I have no doubt , has done this to more than me,” he said. “She’s doing it right now in Greece. I know Corey Lewandowski did this stuff. I know Kristi Noem did this stuff.”

While Deters told MS NOW he would continue to support the president and MAGA candidates in elections, he “cannot stand Trump personally.”

“One, I like most of his policies. Two, I cannot stand his megalomania, his egomania, his, you know, Mount Rushmore talk and arch talk,” Deters said, adding that he does support the president’s White House ballroom project .

“Donald Trump loves billionaires and any MAGA politician,” the donor continued. “He doesn’t care about average rank-and-file people unless they’re for his votes.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.
