articles.title: Shock poll: 89 percent of boomers want higher taxes on young people
articles.summary: It’s simply wrong to sentence the next generation to indentured servitude.
articles.body:
If you spent any time on social media this week, you might have seen a trending news item that really boils my blood, and maybe yours: The headline is this:

“JUST IN: 89% of American seniors support higher taxes on younger workers to protect current Social Security benefits, per Cato Institute”

And that got shared over and over by all sorts of different accounts. In fact, it isn’t breaking news — I tracked down the Cato Institute study that produced this result, and it was published last December .

But aside from the false portrayal of this as breaking news, I totally agree with the freakout and the fury it produced on social media. Yes, it is a moral scandal that the boomers — retirees, the wealthiest generation in American history — will stop at nothing to protect their welfare payments from the government, and would be happy to raise taxes on younger, poorer Americans in order to save Social Security.

From Cato: “A striking generational divide emerges over Social Security reform. A majority (53%) of Americans under age 30 say younger workers should be protected from higher taxes even if doing so requires reducing benefits for current retirees. In sharp contrast, 89% of seniors age 65 and older believe current retirees’ benefits should be protected even if that means higher taxes on younger workers.”

When Social Security was enacted nearly 100 years ago, it was necessary to prevent people who were too old to work from dying of poverty on the streets. But the situation is very different today. Now, it is elder Americans who own most of the wealth in society.

And they have been able to rig the system to protect their largesse. We have a housing shortage because they support zoning laws that make it difficult to build new houses, for instance. In fact, so many of the things young people need — housing, childcare, medical care, education, jobs — are made less obtainable because government regulation gets in the way. Regulation supported by the boomers.

And now they want to raise our taxes too?

It’s generational theft. Keep in mind, no one is going to raise their taxes. Both Republicans and Democrats are actually competing to make the elderly pay less in taxes, including by eliminating property taxes for them — but not for you, first-time homebuyer.

And some conservative commentators, to their credit, recognize it as absurd. On X, Matt Walsh writes :

“I understand that the social security conversation is political poison. But I’m not running for office so I don’t care about that. Taking huge chunks out of the paychecks of young working Americans in order to pay for the retirements of older Americans who have a net worth several times higher, all to prop up a system that everyone knows likely won’t be there when those younger people are retirement age themselves, is morally abhorrent and economically insane. Everyone knows it, too, but we’re held hostage by elderly politicians who refuse to surrender power, and older voters who, as a group (with exceptions, obviously), simply don’t care all that much about the financial and cultural future their grandchildren will inherit.”

On the other hand, if older Americans are actually determined to maintain their current Social Security payouts, it’s going to mean a lot more taxes for everyone else. Jessica Reidl, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, has done the math.

She writes : “Maintaining full Social Security benefits would mean raising the payroll tax from 12.4% to nearly 17%. Also fully funding Medicare would require adding another 9pp, or perhaps adding a 25% VAT. So that (often wealthy) seniors can keep getting back far more than they paid in.”

That’s right, they’re getting much more than they paid in, because they live longer on average than was considered normal at the time the program was designed. This is simply unworkable. It’s bankrupting our country and it’s dooming our children and our grandchildren. We need more people, hopefully more politicians, to stand up and say enough is enough, even though it’s politically unpopular.

It’s simply wrong to sentence the next generation to indentured servitude.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: DeSantis fraud crackdown drives nearly $1B spending plunge after providers billed impossible hours
articles.summary: Florida's Medicaid fraud crackdown uncovered providers billing for more than 24 hours a day, driving a nearly $1 billion drop in ABA therapy spending.
articles.body: Florida's sweeping Medicaid fraud crackdown has helped drive a nearly $1 billion reduction in projected annual spending on behavioral therapy services alone, according to state officials, after investigators uncovered suspicious billing practices. Tallahassee’s internal crackdown — which included discoveries of providers billing Medicaid for more hours than there are in a day — comes amid heightened federal scrutiny of Medicaid fraud, including investigations and payment reviews involving Minnesota. The DeSantis administration said its approach aims to stop suspicious Medicaid claims before taxpayer dollars are paid out rather than trying to recover improper payments afterward. The strategy mirrors a call from HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to move away from traditional "pay-and-chase" models. "This year, we announced the most significant Medicaid integrity initiative in the history of our state, and today, I was proud to announce some of the results from these efforts," Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a news release. VANCE TURNS UP HEAT ON STATES WITH FEDERAL CASH THREAT OVER MEDICAID FRAUD CRACKDOWN More than 220 Medicaid providers have been terminated for fraud, waste or abuse, while more than 260 have faced payment restrictions or suspensions. The state has also referred more than 150 suspected fraud cases to the attorney general's office over the past year. Annual Medicaid spending on Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA), a therapy commonly used for children with autism, had been projected to reach $3.86 billion but is now expected to total $2.88 billion in fiscal year 2026-27, according to the governor's office. Officials attributed the nearly $980 million reduction to a combination of fraud enforcement, managed care and utilization management efforts. Florida's Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA) told Fox News Digital that its expanded monitoring uncovered providers billing Medicaid for services through every weekend and holiday for months, including instances in which providers billed for more than 24 hours of services in a single day. "Protecting Medicaid means protecting the people it was created to serve," AHCA Secretary Shevaun Harris said in a statement. FRAUD EXPERT EXPOSES HOW HIDDEN NETWORKS DROVE MINNESOTA FRAUD, OTHER MAJOR SCAMS: 'CRIMINAL ENTERPRISE' "For children, pregnant women, the disabled, and our seniors, it means making sure they have access to high-quality care while ensuring taxpayer dollars are not lost to fraud or abuse. AHCA will continue taking decisive action to strengthen program integrity, hold bad actors accountable and safeguard these critical services for Floridians," she said. Harris’ agency provided additional details on its crackdown to Fox News Digital, including how its new fraud-protection mechanisms work. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Through a pilot program with identity-verification firm SentiLink, Florida is screening for stolen or fake identities and hidden ownership structures among Medicaid providers. Separately, the state has imposed enrollment moratoriums on certain high-risk provider categories. AHCA also told Fox News Digital that it has issued more than 1,000 adverse decisions involving Medicaid provider enrollment or re-enrollment since January 2026, part of its effort to prevent suspicious providers from entering or remaining in the program. The agency has conducted 400 site visits to providers since January, including providers in high-risk categories such as applied behavior analysis, medical equipment and adult day care. "Medicaid fraud is a national problem, and it is growing more sophisticated everywhere," AHCA told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Florida is not waiting to be told what to do. We are building the model: prevent fraud at the front door, verify every provider, and follow the data. We welcome partnership with CMS and other states, because a fraudulent provider stopped in Florida is a scheme that does not move on to the next state."

articles.title: ICE tried using Palantir to review voter roll information?
articles.summary: ICE is now investigating the people who help Americans register to vote.
articles.body:
ICE is now investigating the people who help Americans register to vote.

According to internal government documents obtained by the legal nonprofit Democracy Forward, Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative arm, spent the past year scrutinizing hundreds of nonprofits and organizations involved in voter registration , including at least 82 organizations in Pennsylvania and 41 in New Jersey.

These documents were obtained through a recent Freedom of Information Act lawsuit, and they show the agency considered using undercover agents to communicate with organizations suspected of helping noncitizens register to vote.

A June report says investigators had taken in 50.6 million records from a Justice Department dataset, plus another 48.4 million records obtained through what the document calls “independent sources.” That’s nearly 100 million records being analyzed for potential investigative leads. This year, Homeland Security Investigations said it had opened 418 voter-fraud cases, but 318 of those 418 cases had not been referred for prosecution — meaning a lot of the investigations reportedly produced nothing.

According to the documents, Homeland Security Investigations focused on nonprofit groups in battleground states like Ohio and Pennsylvania, as well as targeting places like Washington, D.C., and Minnesota.

State voter-roll information may have also been entered into Palantir’s ELITE system , an ICE tool used to identify, prioritize and locate people targeted for immigration enforcement, according to Democracy Docket.

Noncitizen voting is already prohibited under federal law. The government was not investigating a person suspected of illegally voting, which would have been valid — it was investigating the organizations helping people register to vote. Which should be problematic for everyone.

This administration has a documented history of challenging the legitimacy of our elections. Don’t forget, Donald Trump pressured Georgia officials after losing the 2020 election, and asked Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find” enough votes to reverse his defeat. To this day, the president won’t even admit he lost the the 2020 election.

Now, years later, his administration has built an enormous federal apparatus around finding voter fraud, which now apparently includes examining nonprofits, scrutinizing voter rolls and considering undercover operations.

The available evidence shows that voter fraud is extraordinarily rare. One Brennan Center study of 23.5 million votes across 42 jurisdictions, found just 30 suspected cases of voter fraud. Thirty — that’s roughly one for every million votes. More recent state audits have similarly found numbers that were extremely low and did not sway the outcome of the election in any way.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Vance signals discomfort after report alleges Kimberly Guilfoyle tried to exchange access for funds
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he took issue with anyone seeking financial gain in exchange for access to Trump administration officials after a repor...
articles.body:
Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he took issue with anyone seeking financial gain in exchange for access to Trump administration officials after a report claimed Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece, sought funds and offered access to top administration officials ahead of her confirmation.

"Obviously I don't love that," Vance said when a reporter asked whether he had any reaction to a scenario where an American ambassador tried to exchange access for funds. The reporter did not name Guilfoyle specifically.

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Guilfoyle had asked a donor and former congressional candidate for $100,000 to pay off an American Express bill. CNN has reached out to Guilfoyle. A lawyer for the ambassador told the Journal that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages.

Vance, who said he was unsure of the specifics of the episode, reserved further comment during a press conference on visa fraud.

But the vice president said in general he was uncomfortable with access-for-pay schemes.

"Of course I don't like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official," he said.

"But you know, I assume you're talking about a specific case, and I can't say with confidence that the case you're talking about is actually reflective of of the way you're describing it," he added.

According to the Journal, the donor, Eric Deters, had been seeking Guilfoyle's help in "getting the attention of the new Trump administration on some personal tax and legal issues."

"Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," Guilfoyle texted Deters days ahead of her confirmation hearing, according to the Journal. Deters didn't make the payment, the newspaper reported.

Guilfoyle had been with Secretary of State Marco Rubio as he visited Greece and gave a major policy speech this week.

When asked about the Journal reporting earlier on Thursday, Rubio refused to comment.

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," Rubio said before he boarded his plane to leave the country, with Guilfoyle looking on.

Guilfoyle was nominated to the role in Athens by President Donald Trump in December 2024, prior to him taking office.

She had been engaged to Donald Trump Jr. and is close to the Trump family.

Guilfoyle is a former co-host of Fox News' "The Five" and was an assistant district attorney at the San Francisco and Los Angeles district attorneys' offices before beginning her media career.

She abruptly left her position on Fox News in July 2018 and later served as the Trump campaign's finance chair during his 2020 presidential bid. She later became a key witness to the events leading up to the US Capitol attack on January 6, 2021, and met with the House select committee investigating the insurrection in 2022. In addition to her role on Trump's campaign, Guilfoyle also helped raise money for organizers leading up to the "Stop the Steal" rally on January 6.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Schumer, Jeffries dodge Mamdani controversy as fellow New York Dem unloads
articles.summary: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's Oct. 7 anniversary statement drew sharp criticism, but Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries have stayed notably silent.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has come under fire for his comments on the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, but two leading voices in New York politics have so far remained quiet. Mamdani’s post on Wednesday briefly acknowledged Hamas’ blitz on Israel that left more than 1,100 Israelis dead and more than 250 others captured and held hostage by the terrorist organization. But the bulk of his statement spent time on criticizing Israel for its actions in Gaza in the three years since. "The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children," Mamdani said on X. "Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed." MAMDANI DOUBLES DOWN ON ANTI-ISRAEL OCT 7 STATEMENT AFTER BACKLASH "That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing," he continued. "Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes." Mamdani notably did not mention the Jewish community in New York City, which is home to nearly 1 million Jews, according to a 2023 study from the UJA-Federation of New York. And while at least one New York Democrat, Rep. Dan Goldman, laid into Mamdani for his comments, neither Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer nor House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the two most powerful Democrats in Congress, has reacted. MAMDANI’S $30M PLAN TO FIGHT ANTISEMITISM INCLUDES INCREASED FUNDING FOR ANTI-ISRAEL GROUP "This is a reprehensible statement on the anniversary of the horrific terrorist attack by a Palestinian terrorist organization against innocent Israelis," Goldman said on X. "In the guise of ‘grieving’ with those mourning that day, Mayor Mamdani asserts as fact hotly disputed allegations that he knows full well will offend and further upset those same people he pretends to grieve with." Neither Schumer nor Jeffries responded to requests for comment on Mamdani's remarks. They put out their own statements on the Oct. 7 attack on Wednesday. Schumer, who is Jewish, noted that the attack was the "single deadliest day in Jewish history since the Holocaust." His support of Israel has become a wedge issue for some Senate Democrats, who have slowly pushed back against funding arms for Israel following three years of conflict in Gaza. DEM SENATOR WHO DEMANDED SAUDI ACCOUNTABILITY OVER KHASHOGGI MEETS WITH CROWN PRINCE, PUSHES PALESTINIAN STATE "Today, we reaffirm our commitment to the security of the Israeli people, to the aid and wellbeing of the Palestinian people and the recovery of the devastation in Gaza that the ensuing conflict brought, and to doubling down on efforts for a lasting peace resulting in two states where Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side in equal measures of peace, security, dignity, and mutual recognition," Schumer said. Jeffries was more aligned with Schumer’s left flank in his statement, while recognizing that "we are reminded of the painful reality that the Jewish people are in a constant struggle for survival, as has been the case for thousands of years." articles.title: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
articles.summary: An international visa program has for years allowed US tech companies to hire highly skilled workers from abroad.
articles.body:
Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.

Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents.

Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants."

Microsoft said most of the H1b visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff.

"No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.

He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.

The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference.

Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers.

The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment.

The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped at 85,000 per year.

A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide.

Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages.

The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires.

She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive.

According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary for an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000.

"We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said.

Satya Nadella, Microsoft's longtime CEO, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump.

Nadella was also present at other recent White House events, including a luncheon on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping.

Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday.

"Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.

He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US.

Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating that grace period altogether.

Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more.

None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments.

The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades.

The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely.

During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories.

images.caption: The White House has often made extreme claims regarding international workers and immigration.

articles.title: Trump’s rekindled alliance with Elon Musk on display at medal ceremony
articles.summary: President Trump heaped praise on Elon Musk on Thursday as he awarded the tech leader with the National Medal of Science, just a little more than a year after the high-profile relationship between the pair turned into an explosive public feud. Trump presented the SpaceX and Tesla CEO with the nation’s highest form of recognition…
articles.body:
President Trump heaped praise on Elon Musk on Thursday as he awarded the tech leader with the National Medal of Science , just a little more than a year after the high-profile relationship between the pair turned into an explosive public feud.

Trump presented the SpaceX and Tesla CEO with the nation’s highest form of recognition for scientists and engineers, touting him as a “national treasure” and “our modern-day Thomas Edison.”

“Quite honestly there’s nobody like him,” the president said. “Few Americans in history have done more to advance America’s national interest and Elon, in one field after another, his genius and determination have made science fiction into reality.”

The award comes a little more than a year after Trump and Musk — who once referred to himself as the “first buddy” — were embroiled in a public falling out over provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Musk took on a prominent role in the administration after spending at least $250 million to boost Trump’s 2024 campaign. He was tapped to lead the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a highly controversial cost-cutting effort.

The tech billionaire left the White House after just four months, as cracks appeared in his relationship with the president that eventually spilled out onto social media, with Musk threatening to launch a third party.

However, the two reached a detente of sorts following the September 2025 assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Trump and Musk were both seen sitting together at Kirk’s memorial service.

Musk has since appeared with Trump at a number of major events, including the president’s state visit to China in May as well as Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last month.

He was also among the tech leaders present at the White House for Trump’s artificial intelligence summit, where the president invited Musk to speak to reporters during a rare appearance on the White House North Lawn.

Trump also honored Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google co-founder Sergey Brin and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su with the National Medal of Science on Thursday, while presenting Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

articles.title: Who is Eric Deters? The MAGA donor Kimberly Guilfoyle sought $100,000 from for AmEx bill
articles.summary: Eric Deters, a former Kentucky congressional candidate and longtime ally of President Trump, has emerged in the national spotlight after an explosive report revealed his alleged text exchanges with U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle over her credit card debt. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Guilfoyle, ex-wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D)…
articles.body:
Eric Deters, a former Kentucky congressional candidate and longtime ally of President Trump, has emerged in the national spotlight after an explosive report revealed his alleged text exchanges with U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle over her credit card debt.

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Guilfoyle, ex-wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and the former fiancee of Donald Trump Jr., allegedly pressed Deters to pay her $100,000 American Express balance without leaving a paper trail, and in exchange promised to help him reach senior administration officials.

Deters, 63, is a former attorney, businessman and conservative radio host who has spent years building connections within Trump’s inner circle. He declined to make the payment, and has since publicly accused Guilfoyle of offering political access in exchange for large sums of money.

Guilfoyle’s dealings with Deters began drawing attention after the Journal obtained hundreds of text messages, emails and letters, detailing their relationship in a bombshell report.

According to the outlet, Guilfoyle told Deters she needed the balance to be paid ahead of her July 9, 2025, confirmation hearing before the Senate.

“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote in one exchange on the messaging app Signal, which was obtained by the Journal. The message was sent on July 3, days before her hearing.

She then reportedly sent Deters instructions to wire $100,000 directly to her American Express account, suggesting the payment would not leave a paper trail.

“It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” she wrote. “Please.”

Deters refused, telling Guilfoyle he did not have the money and could not make the payment without jeopardizing his marriage.

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle repeatedly urged Deters not to document their financial arrangements in writing, warning that doing so could threaten her ambassadorship.

In an interview with ABC’s “Good Morning America” on Thursday, Deters characterized their relationship as a “quid pro quo,” alleging that Guilfoyle promised to use her political connections to help him if he provided the money.

“She made it very clear, and the text messages make it very clear, she was so desperate for me to send that $100,000,” Deters said, claiming that Guilfoyle offered to become his “ride or die in the Trump world” if he paid her.

Guilfoyle’s attorney has since disputed the authenticity of the messages without identifying specific inaccuracies, saying she was owed money for previous speaking engagements and travel expenses — a claim Deters denied.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has since refused to comment on the story, telling reporters while on diplomatic travel in Greece that he does not know if the allegations are “true or not true.”

“Our job is not to respond every time someone decides to give the media something without any advance warning, without having any chance to look at it and see what’s in there,” Rubio said.

Deters has been an outspoken supporter of Trump since he first campaigned for president in 2016, promoting Trump’s candidacy as a morning radio host based in Ohio.

He frequently declared himself “Trump today, Trump tomorrow, Trump forever,” according to the Journal.

His connections to Trump’s family grew through Freedom Fest, a conservative gathering he launched in Northern Kentucky in 2020 in opposition to COVID-19 mandates.

The event attracted prominent figures in Trump’s inner circle, including the president’s sons Eric Trump and Trump Jr., as well as Guilfoyle, who got engaged to Trump Jr. that same year before the couple announced their breakup in 2024.

Deters told the Journal he paid Guilfoyle $300,000 over several years to speak at the event, along with $200,000 to Trump Jr. and $100,000 to Eric Trump.

He also donated $125,000 to the MAGA Inc. super PAC, according to Federal Election Commission records.

The event continued for several years, though its 2026 edition was canceled after organizers sold just six of the 100 available VIP tickets, according to Deters . In September, he said on Facebook that he is “never ever, ever, ever ever doing this event again.”

After Trump’s 2024 election victory, Deters began seeking Guilfoyle’s help with several disputes involving federal agencies.

One involved an Ohio spine surgeon named Abubakar Atiq Durrani, who fled to Pakistan after facing charges of performing unnecessary surgeries and defrauding insurance companies.

Deters, who said he was advising attorneys representing hundreds of Durrani’s former patients, wanted the Justice Department to pursue his extradition.

He also sought assistance with an Internal Revenue Service inquiry into a tax deduction connected to the sale of his interest in the family business.

According to the Journal, Guilfoyle contacted then-IRS Commissioner Billy Long on Deters’ behalf and discussed reaching other senior administration officials.

Deters also offered to pay her $1 million if she could arrange an interview with podcaster Tucker Carlson, hoping to draw attention to the Durrani case. The interview never materialized.

Deters told the Journal that despite his financial contributions and connections, Guilfoyle failed to deliver on her promises, which included lobbying top Trump officials such as FBI director Kash Patel and former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

“She never came through on anything,” he said.

Political career and legal controversies

Deters launched several unsuccessful bids for political office, including for Kentucky governor and Congress, where he challenged Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) in the state’s 4th Congressional District.

The Northern Kentucky businessman, who previously co-owned regional restaurant chain Snappy Tomato Pizza, was also a former criminal defense attorney.

His legal career was marked by repeated disciplinary proceedings. In 2020, Deters was banned from entering a courthouse in Hamilton County, Ohio, after threatening on social media to burn it down.

The Kentucky Bar Association also twice suspended him over misconduct, including making false statements in court proceedings and filing frivolous claims.

The Kentucky Supreme Court rejected his effort to regain his license to practice law in 2021, with the chief justice describing his approach to practicing law as “anarchy.”

“Deters’ lack of self-awareness is utterly amazing,” the opinion reads.

Deters has since retired from practicing law, describing himself to the Journal as a “legal outlaw.”

articles.title: Roberts halts imminent deadline for FCC to rule on Democrats’ TV ad rate challenge
articles.summary: Chief Justice John Roberts halted, for now, a deadline for the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to rule on Democrats’ challenge to a policy giving party committees access to cheaper television ad rates in the lead-up to the midterms. A lower court had ordered the FCC to decide the challenge by Friday, but the Trump administration has…
articles.body:
Chief Justice John Roberts halted, for now, a deadline for the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to rule on Democrats’ challenge to a policy giving party committees access to cheaper television ad rates in the lead-up to the midterms.

A lower court had ordered the FCC to decide the challenge by Friday, but the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to stave off the deadline using its emergency docket. The justices already intervened in Republicans’ favor once before.

Roberts’s order halts the imminent deadline until the Supreme Court rules. The chief justice received the request by default but could ultimately refer the matter to the full court for a vote.

He has ordered the Democratic candidates suing to respond by Saturday evening.

The administration’s bid is backed by Republicans’ Senate and House campaign arms, which boast a cash advantage and hope to use the policy to bolster their chances in holding onto control of Congress in November’s contests.

The legal battle concerns a federal mandate that broadcast stations offer their lowest-available advertising rate to campaigns in the 60 days preceding a general election.

Everyone agrees candidates get the discount, but whether political parties and joint fundraising committees can, too, has come under question.

The Supreme Court ruled last month that Democrats needed to wait for the FCC to rule on its challenge before heading to court. The FCC hasn’t done so yet, so the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit accused the agency of dragging its feet and demanded it move along by Friday.

The Trump administration called the judges’ directive a “flagrant abuse.” Republicans’ appeal accused them of attempting an “end run” around the Supreme Court’s previous order.

With 26 days to go until the midterms, the policy allowing party committees to access the cheaper rates remains in effect.

articles.title: White House chief of staff’s daughter shows up in photo from Republicka Srpska
articles.summary: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’s daughter showed up in a photo from Republika Srpska, a small self-governing territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina led by a pro-Russian political party. Katie Wiles, a partner at Continental Strategy, shared photos on social media, appearing to show her holding a rifle while standing next to Željko Budimir,…
articles.body:
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’s daughter showed up in a photo from Republika Srpska, a small self-governing territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina led by a pro-Russian political party.

Katie Wiles, a partner at Continental Strategy, shared photos on social media, appearing to show her holding a rifle while standing next to Željko Budimir, the interior minister of Republika Srpska, according to CBS News .

Wiles wrote, “mostly work + some serious fun,” in the post’s caption.

The images were shared by Albanian American activist Evi Kokalari and reportedly taken in mid-August during a business trip for another client of Continental Strategy.

“Katie Wiles visited the country in mid-August for two days with a U.S.-based company who was invited to do a feasibility study in the region,” a spokesperson said, according to CBS News. “Wiles provides strategic communications support to this US company and has done so for over two years. Wiles has not spoken with any United States Government official regarding Srpska.”

Budimir is a close ally of pro-Russian politician and former Republika Srpska president Milorad Dodik, per CBS News.

This comes after The New York Times reported Tuesday that Chris LaCivita and James Blair, two heads leading Trump’s midterm advertising campaign, were reportedly paid hundreds of thousands of dollars to advise on voting issues in Republicka Srpska.

While The New York Times noted Blair and LaCivita were paid by the government and not the political party behind the government, it wrote that for all intents and purposes work for the government and the party are the same thing.

They were paid through a Washington-based firm ahead of the country’s elections Sunday.

Another one of Dodik’s allies, Zeljka Cvijanovic, took more than 55 percent of votes to be elected to her second term on Bosnia’s tripartite presidency, representing Republika Srpska.

Dodik’s party’s candidate for Republika Srpska’s own president, Savo Minic, also won decisively.

“I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately,” President Trump wrote on Truth Social about Blair and LaCivita.

GOP lawmakers — including Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) — have already condemned the reported ties and demanded further investigation into the allegations.

articles.title: Jeffries vows immediate anti-corruption push next year: ‘Hold the crooks accountable’
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is vowing that Democrats, if they win the House in next month’s midterms, will launch immediate investigations into corruption allegations against President Trump, his family and other associates who have benefited financially during the early years of his second term. “What we’ve seen from the Trump cartel is that…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is vowing that Democrats, if they win the House in next month’s midterms, will launch immediate investigations into corruption allegations against President Trump, his family and other associates who have benefited financially during the early years of his second term.

“What we’ve seen from the Trump cartel is that they’re more focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends and their donors than they are with making life more affordable for the American people,” Jeffries said Thursday during a press conference in his Brooklyn district.

“And our promise to the country in the new Congress is that, beginning on Day 1, we’re going to hold the crooks accountable.”

The remarks come amid a flurry of new reports about administration officials, donors and advisers profiting, or seeking to profit, from their connections to the White House.

Last week, The New York Times reported that the administration’s efforts to broker a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine featured an emerging agreement over Russian oil that’s poised to benefit a billionaire Trump donor and Middle Eastern businessmen with ties to Jared Kushner, the president’s son in law.

On Tuesday, The Times reported that a pair of top campaign advisers, Chris LaCivita and James Blair, had been paid hundreds of thousands of dollars to help reelect right-wing Balkan politicians allied with Russia.

That was followed a day later by a Wall Street Journal report revealing that Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former fiancé of Donald Trump, Jr., and now the U.S. ambassador to Greece, had pressured a wealthy Trump donor to pay off $100,000 in credit card debt in return for political favors.

“It absolutely was a quid pro quo,” the Trump donor, Eric Deters , said Thursday in an interview with MS NOW.

Such episodes have outraged Democrats on and off of Capitol Hill. Many liberals in the party are already pushing for impeachments — a step Jeffries and other Democratic leaders have so far resisted.

Their focus has been to make the campaign a referendum on the high cost of living and economic volatility that’s accompanied Trump’s second term. Party leaders are vowing quick action on a series of legislative fixes — rolling back tariffs, ending the Iran War, reversing Medicaid cuts — designed to ease consumer costs.

But Jeffries’s promise to launch an immediate and parallel effort to investigate potential corruption in the administration aims to ease the liberals’ concerns, sending a message that the economic focus won’t distract from efforts to hold public officials accountable for wrongdoing.

Such investigations have been virtually non-existent while both chambers of Congress have been controlled by Trump’s GOP allies. But the top Democrats on the various investigative committees — most notably the Oversight and Judiciary Committees — are vowing to change that if they get the gavels.

articles.title: At least 81 US aircraft worth up to $3.3bn lost or damaged in Iran war
articles.summary: The damage, documented in a Congressional Budget Office report, comes as Trump faces criticism over war’s cost.
articles.body:
At least 81 United States military aircraft, including fighter jets and drones, have been lost or damaged during Operation Epic Fury, the code name for Washington’s military campaign against Iran launched earlier this year.

The statistic comes as part of a report released on Monday by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), a nonpartisan government agency that provides budget-related research to the legislature.

It estimated that, as of August 1, the cost of the American aircraft losses during the US-Israeli war against Iran was between $1.9bn and $3.3bn.

The report this week highlights the growing price tag for the war, which began on February 28. A lasting ceasefire has remained out of reach as the conflict continues into its eighth month.

“The asymmetries of warfare show that even small countries with small militaries can inflict damage on the world’s best militaries,” said Harlan Ullman, a former naval officer and chairman of the Killowen Group, a government advisory firm.

He told Al Jazeera that Iran has managed to achieve a degree of success in damaging US military hardware and bases in the Middle East.

“Iran has plenty of US targets available, and you can imagine what a small drone can do to a major military asset. We have seen examples of that in the Gulf countries during the conflict,” Ullman explained.

Monday’s report listed 12 F-15E Strike Eagle fighter jets, one F-35A Lightning II jet and seven KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refuelling aircraft among those affected. Forty-five of the 81 aircraft identified in the report were MQ-9 Reaper drones.

Experts like Ullman trace some of the US vulnerabilities to the changing nature of modern warfare, which is increasingly reliant on low-cost drones that are widely available.

Many have pointed to Russia’s war against Ukraine as an example of how a smaller military like Kyiv’s can keep a larger adversary at bay through drone warfare.

Rumours of a potential drone attack on Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford — a British base that has hosted US assets during the Iran war — also resulted in the sudden departure of a dozen US aircraft on Sunday.

Ullman pointed to those instances as examples of how the threat of drone attacks has been effective in putting larger militaries on the defensive.

“We have seen the US had to relocate its B-1 bombers from the UK fearing Iranian attacks, and we have seen how the Ukrainian Operation Spiderweb, where small drones were launched from inside Russia, targeted and destroyed Russian military assets,” Ullman said.

The rising costs associated with the war against Iran have also placed political pressure on the administration of US President Donald Trump.

Earlier this year, his administration requested a record $1.5 trillion in defence spending for fiscal year 2027, citing the demands of the war.

But the soaring price tag has sparked scepticism in Congress, particularly from Democrats.

Last month, 45 Senate Democrats and one independent wrote an open letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth demanding transparent accounting of the war’s costs.

They argued that a “detailed breakdown” of the costs was necessary before Congress considers further supplemental funding.

“American taxpayers have already paid an extra $100 billion out of their pockets for higher gas and diesel prices alone and at least another $60 billion in higher costs for things like groceries, mortgages, and plane tickets as a result of the war,” the senators wrote.

“Now you are asking that they pay again to fund a war of choice that Congress never authorized and the President launched with no strategic plan.”

In a separate report issued in September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the war with Iran has cost roughly $38bn, as of August 1.

That amount reflects the costs of replacing expended munitions and equipment lost in battle, as well as increased fuel costs and other operations.

“An additional month of conflict would cost $2 billion,” the office said.

However, it added that, “if the intensity of the conflict increased to roughly the level experienced in July, the cost per month would increase to $3 billion”.

The Pentagon said it had “nothing further to provide” in a response to Al Jazeera’s query about whether the losses reported this week were expected and how they would impact the department’s budget.

Polls indicate the war is widely unpopular among US voters, and analysts have speculated about whether reports of rising costs may have an impact on the US midterm elections, which will decide whether Trump’s Republican Party will retain control of Congress.

But Ullman is sceptical that reports like Monday’s will be a determining factor in the outcome of the vote.

“I do not think that report will influence the course of the upcoming midterm elections, as many Americans, even those who oppose the war, would see it as expected damage in a military operation,” Ullman said.

articles.title: ‘We don’t want this right now’: James Talarico off the trail with the flu for 12 days
articles.summary: The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now.
articles.body: The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now. But in the final push, when campaigns believe most voters are finally tuning in, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has been off the trail for 12 days. His campaign says he is suffering from the flu and expected to be back in action this weekend. While he has appeared virtually at a forum, Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser and, according to the virtual remarks he gave to the Hispanic Business Council the following day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care. It has all prompted a stream of fodder from his opponent, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose campaign is calling on Talarico to produce a photo of himself with a newspaper showing today’s date. “We have a simple request: proof of life,” Paxton campaign spokeswoman Madison Cercy said. “James Talarico wants to represent 31 million Texans in the U.S. Senate, but for 12 days, he’s hidden from every one of them. There’s a reason they call it ‘Texas Tough,’ and it’s not because Texans hide at the first sign of trouble. If James Talarico is too fragile to face Texans, he has no business asking for their vote.” While some Texas Democrats are shrugging it off, it is causing some consternation. “He’s like, really sick. Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.” Talarico’s absence is undoubtedly a curveball for Democrats who believe his best asset is connecting with potential voters in person. It also presents a turnaround for Talarico, who had been visible in the early days of the campaign as Paxton was off the trail. “After holding more than 100 public events and shaking tens of thousands of hands, James came down with the flu but will be back on the trail this weekend,” Talarico spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement. “Ken Paxton has been ignoring Texans this entire campaign, and his priorities are clear: he doesn’t answer to the people of this state — he answers to his billionaire megadonors and special interests.” Democratic political strategist Ed Espinoza said that some supporters he’s spoken to noted his absence from in-person campaign events and lamented that they wanted to make sure other people were seeing enough of him. Espinoza, though, said he didn’t think that would be a problem. “Look, he’s got like $80 million of ads going right now. So I think that’s pretty good scale for him at the moment,” Espinoza said. “He may be recovering at home, but he is still everywhere.” Espinoza said that he’d rather Talarico be off the trail and recovering now rather than be hampered even closer to the election. Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder said Paxton “caught a little bit of a break” with Talarico’s absence. “It’s certainly not ideal, but we want to make sure he does everything he needs to to make sure that he’s healthy and ready to go. We’re in the homestretch, and it sounds like he’s on the mend, and that’s great news,” Scudder said. “He’s a phenomenal candidate, he’s been working really hard for a long time, and everyone gets sick every now and then.” To Talarico’s great fortune, distractions have abounded. A steady flow of damaging audio featuring Paxton saying that Trump’s midterm convention wasn’t helpful or that cuts to “mandatory spending” were inevitable has grabbed public attention. At the same time, both Paxton and Trump have hit Talarico for being off the trail. “You haven’t seen him in a couple of weeks,” Trump said at a Wednesday rally in San Antonio. “I hear the guy has disappeared. Nobody knows. You know where he is?
